questions.question:
The flowchart is used to identify an unknown pathogen, but some labels are missing.

Which of the following rows correctly identifies the missing labels?

| | W | X | Y | Z |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | Proteins | Viruses | Prokaryotes | Eukaryotes |
| (B) | Prions | Viruses | Bacteria | Fungi |
| (C) | Viruses | Proteins | Prokaryotes | Fungi |
| (D) | Viruses | Prions | Fungi | Bacteria |
questions.answer: Non-cellular pathogens without nucleic acid are prions (W); those with nucleic acid are viruses (X). Of the cellular pathogens, microscopic organisms without membrane-bound organelles are bacteria (Y) and microscopic eukaryotes with a chitin cell wall are fungi (Z).
options: Row A
Row B
Row C
Row D

questions.question: Which of the following diagrams best represents the arrangement of DNA in a prokaryotic cell?
questions.answer: A prokaryote has no nucleus: its DNA is a single circular loop lying free in the cytoplasm (option A).
options: Diagram A: a single loop of DNA, no nucleus
Diagram B: strands of DNA, with a nucleus
Diagram C: a single loop of DNA, with a nucleus
Diagram D: strands of DNA, no nucleus

questions.question:
A section of DNA was sequenced:

ATT AGC CGC

Which is the corresponding strand of mRNA?
questions.answer: mRNA is complementary to the template strand and has uracil in place of thymine: A$\to$U, T$\to$A, G$\to$C, C$\to$G, giving UAA UCG GCG. Options B and C contain thymine, which is not in RNA.
options: CGG CAU UAU
GCC GTA ATA
TAA TCG GCG
UAA UCG GCG

questions.question:
The table shows the changes in the human body when an individual begins exercising.

The following steps are processes in the stimulus-response pathway.

| Step | Process |
|---|---|
| I | Nerves send a signal about lower blood pH to the brain |
| II | Nerves send a signal to an effector |
| III | Chemoreceptors detect a decrease in blood pH |
| IV | Muscles in the pulmonary system (diaphragm) contract and relax at a faster rate, returning oxygen and carbon dioxide to optimum levels |

What is the correct order of steps to explain the changes in the human body when an individual begins exercising?
questions.answer: Stimulus $\to$ receptor $\to$ control centre $\to$ effector $\to$ response: chemoreceptors detect the pH drop (III), signal the brain (I), the brain signals the effector (II), and the muscles respond (IV).
options: III, IV, I, II
I, II, III, IV
III, I, II, IV
III, II, I, IV

questions.question: Which graph depicts the adaptive immune system response after a primary and secondary exposure to a pathogen?
questions.answer: The primary response is slow, with a lag, and produces a low antibody level. The secondary response (due to memory cells) is faster, higher and longer lasting.
options: ![Graph A](assets/img/bio-2022-manly/q5a.png)
![Graph B](assets/img/bio-2022-manly/q5b.png)
![Graph C](assets/img/bio-2022-manly/q5c.png)
![Graph D](assets/img/bio-2022-manly/q5d.png)

questions.question: A healthy couple have a child affected by a rare autosomal recessive disease that develops when the child is 12 years old. What is the probability that the couple's next child will develop this disease?
questions.answer: Both parents must be carriers ($Aa \times Aa$). Each child has a $\frac14 = 25\%$ chance of being $aa$, regardless of earlier children.

questions.question:
Equine influenza (EI) is an acute, highly contagious, viral disease in horses. EI is exotic to Australia and would have a major impact if established here. Humans do not get infected but can physically carry the virus on their skin, hair, clothing and shoes, and can transfer the virus to other horses.

An outbreak of equine influenza is detected in central NSW after the import of breeding stallions.

What step should be taken first to bring the outbreak under control?
questions.answer: The first priority is to stop the virus spreading: restricting horse movement (quarantine and movement controls) contains the outbreak while testing, vaccination and hygiene measures are organised.
options: Introduce mandatory testing for all horses in NSW
Restrict the movement of all horses, particularly into or out of the affected areas
Vaccinate all horses in the Sydney area
Introduce strict hygiene protocols for handling and moving all animals

questions.question: A single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) is a small genetic change, or variation, that can occur within a DNA sequence. The study of SNPs in a population of organisms could be used to gain information on:
questions.answer: SNP patterns are inherited, so comparing them shows how closely related individuals or populations are.
options: physical variation in the population
the physical shape of the DNA present in this organism
the effects of the environment on physical characteristics
relationships between organisms in the population

questions.question:
A medical team is assessing the number of people in a population who are likely to get the symptoms of a disease as a result of exposure to a pathogen. Members of the population are allocated to the quadrants shown in the diagram.

Which row of the table gives the correct assessment of who is most and least likely to get symptoms?

| | Most likely to get symptoms | Least likely to get symptoms |
|---|---|---|
| (A) | Quadrant 2 | Quadrant 3 |
| (B) | Quadrant 1 | Quadrant 2 |
| (C) | Quadrant 1 | Quadrant 4 |
| (D) | Quadrant 3 | Quadrant 2 |
questions.answer: Quadrant 1 is the group that is both exposed and susceptible, so it is the most likely to develop symptoms. Quadrant 4 is neither exposed nor susceptible, so it is the least likely.
options: Row A
Row B
Row C
Row D

questions.question: Which of the following best describes 'gene cloning'?
questions.answer: Gene cloning makes many identical copies of one particular gene, usually by inserting it into a plasmid that is replicated by bacteria.
options: Occurs in nature
Gives multiple copies of the same gene
Gives multiple copies of different genes
Is a simple, one-stage process

questions.question:
Aboriginal Australians have a rich and detailed knowledge of native Australian plants. Scientists are now discovering that many bioactive compounds found in plants are effective antimicrobial agents. An experiment was conducted to determine the effectiveness of three Australian plant extracts against the bacterium *Bacillus subtilis*. The results are shown below.

Which of the following conclusions can be drawn from the results?
questions.answer: *Bacillus subtilis* is a bacterium, so compounds that kill it are antibacterial (antibiotic). The clear zones of inhibition around the *Eucalyptus* and *Banksia* extracts show these extracts are effective. Antifungal compounds would not be tested by a bacterial culture.
options: *Eucalyptus major* leaf extract and *Banksia citriodora* leaf extract contain antibiotic compounds that are effective against *Bacillus subtilis*.
*Eucalyptus major* leaf extract and *Banksia citriodora* leaf extract contain antifungal compounds that are effective against *Bacillus subtilis*.
*Macadamia integrifolia* leaf extract contains antibiotic compounds but they are not effective against *Bacillus subtilis*.
*Macadamia integrifolia* leaf extract contains antifungal compounds but they are not effective against *Bacillus subtilis*.

questions.question:
Myrtle rust (*Puccinia psidii*) is a fungal disease that attacks the soft, actively growing leaves, shoot tips and young stems of *Eucalyptus* and other Myrtaceae plants. The disease produces small purple spots which later develop masses of bright yellow spores.

Eucalypts have a number of mechanisms that help them resist or respond to infection by myrtle rust. They have thick bark and cell walls reinforced with pectin and lignin. Leaves produce eucalyptus oil, which has antifungal properties. When receptors on the eucalypt's cell walls detect fungal markers, those cells produce more structural protein to reinforce their cell walls. Cells inside the plant showing fungal antigens are flooded with oxygen, increasing their rate of respiration and causing them to 'burn up'.

Which of the following is a general induced response of eucalyptus to the myrtle rust fungus?
questions.answer: An induced response only occurs after the pathogen is detected. Producing extra structural protein is triggered by detecting fungal markers; thick bark, cell walls and eucalyptus oil are always present (pre-existing defences).
options: The thick bark and thick cell walls
The production of eucalyptus oils
The production of structural protein
The actively growing leaves, shoot tips and young stems

questions.question: In 2021 a massive coral spawning event occurred in the Great Barrier Reef, where all coral species released their eggs and sperm at the same time. What form of reproduction is spawning?
questions.answer: Eggs and sperm (gametes) are released into the water and fuse outside the body: sexual reproduction with external fertilisation.
options: Asexual, budding
Asexual, binary fission
Sexual, internal fertilisation
Sexual, external fertilisation

questions.question:
The diagram shows the original sequence of a stretch of a chromosome and four possible types of mutations (P, Q, R and S).

Which row of the table correctly identifies each type of mutation?

| | Mutation P | Mutation Q | Mutation R | Mutation S |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | Translocation | Duplication | Deletion | Inversion |
| (B) | Inversion | Duplication | Deletion | Translocation |
| (C) | Translocation | Inversion | Deletion | Duplication |
| (D) | Inversion | Duplication | Translocation | Deletion |
questions.answer: P: a segment is reversed (inversion). Q: a segment is repeated (duplication). R: a segment is lost (deletion). S: a segment moves to a different chromosome (translocation).
options: Row A
Row B
Row C
Row D

questions.question: Errors in the production of insulin by the pancreas can cause serious metabolic disorders in the body. Which of the following is NOT a consequence of increased insulin concentration in the blood?
questions.answer: Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting glycogen formation, glucose uptake by muscle and fat cells and conversion of glucose to fat. It is not linked to increased polypeptide synthesis in the liver.
options: increased synthesis of polypeptides in the liver
increased production of glycogen by the liver
increased uptake of glucose by muscle and fat cells
increased conversion of glucose to fat in fat cells

questions.question:
The diagram shows homologous chromosomes as two pairs of sister chromatids labelled with alleles A and a, B and b, and C and c.

Which of the series of chromatids below would be the product of this process?
questions.answer: Crossing over exchanges segments between chromatids of the homologous pair, so all four chromatids are recombinant: two with $A\ldots b$ (Abc, AbC) and two with $a\ldots B$ (aBc, aBC).
options: AbC, Abc, aBC, aBc
ABC, ABc, abC, abc
ABc, ABc, abC, abC
Abc, AbC, aBc, aBC

questions.question: This image represents a genetic phenomenon. Name this phenomenon.
questions.answer: A random event (here a land mass) changes allele frequencies by chance in a small, isolated group: genetic drift.
options: Mutation
Gene flow
Genetic drift
Gene variation

questions.question:
This map shows the percentage of children aged between 6 months and 5 years who had received vitamin A supplementation in 2014 (adapted from World Bank).

Which is the main limitation with the data provided in the diagram?
questions.answer: Many countries are shaded as having no data, so the picture is incomplete. The other statements describe the scope of the data, not a limitation.
options: The map does not provide any adult data
There is no data given for many countries
It only shows vitamin A supplementation

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct with regard to the difference between germline and somatic mutations?
questions.answer: Germline mutations occur in gametes (or their precursors) and can be passed to offspring; somatic mutations occur in body cells and are not inherited.
options: Genetic disease that develops during a person's lifetime can only result from somatic mutations
Somatic mutations affect DNA and germline mutations affect mRNA
Both germline mutations and somatic mutations are heritable
Germline mutations are heritable and somatic mutations are not.

questions.question:
Animals and plants reproduce in different ways.

Hormones play an important role in the pregnancy of mammals. Outline the role of a named hormone in pregnancy and how the hormone's level changes during pregnancy.
questions.answer: **Progesterone** keeps the endometrium thick and intact, maintains the placenta and reduces contractions of the uterus. Its level rises throughout the first 36-38 weeks of pregnancy and then falls towards birth. (Oestrogen, oxytocin or prolactin are also acceptable.)

questions.question:
Animals and plants reproduce in different ways.

Plants can reproduce either sexually or asexually. Draw a table that contrasts these reproduction methods by providing at least THREE characteristics for each type of reproduction.
questions.answer:
| Characteristic | Sexual reproduction | Asexual reproduction |
|---|---|---|
| Parents | (usually) two | one |
| New plants made from | seeds | the original plant, not seeds |
| Offspring | genetically different | genetically identical |
| Energy needed | more | less |
| Gametes | needed | not needed |

questions.question:
Part of a model of a negative feedback loop is shown (stimulus $\to$ receptor $\to$ X $\to$ effector).

What occurs at X?
questions.answer: The message from the receptor goes via the sensory neuron to the central nervous system (control centre), where it is interpreted and a response is determined and sent to the effector via a motor neuron.

questions.question:
Part of a model of a negative feedback loop is shown (stimulus $\to$ receptor $\to$ X $\to$ effector).

If the effector is a gland, how will the effector respond?
questions.answer: The gland will release a **hormone**.

questions.question:
Part of a model of a negative feedback loop is shown (stimulus $\to$ receptor $\to$ X $\to$ effector).

Using an example, describe how this pathway achieves a negative feedback loop.
questions.answer: If the stimulus is an increase in environmental temperature, **thermoreceptors** detect the change and send a message to the hypothalamus/central nervous system. The CNS determines that **vasodilation** and **sweating** are needed so heat is lost. This reduces body temperature, which negates the original stimulus, returning the body to its set point (homeostasis).

questions.question:
The diagram shows a simplified overview of polypeptide synthesis (DNA $\to$ step X $\to$ RNA $\to$ step Y $\to$ polypeptide).

Identify steps X and Y in the diagram and outline what occurs during these stages.
questions.answer:
Step X is **transcription** and step Y is **translation**.

*Transcription* occurs in the nucleus. Helicase and RNA polymerase unwind and unzip a length of DNA and one strand acts as the template. Free RNA nucleotides pair with the complementary bases of this strand to form messenger RNA (mRNA), which detaches and leaves the nucleus. The DNA then rejoins.

*Translation* occurs at a ribosome in the cytoplasm. The mRNA codons pair with the complementary anticodons of tRNA molecules, each carrying a specific amino acid. The amino acids are joined by peptide bonds until a chain (polypeptide) forms, which is released into the cytoplasm.

questions.question:
The diagram shows a simplified overview of polypeptide synthesis.

Assess the importance of polypeptides.
questions.answer: Polypeptides are long chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Proteins are made of one or more polypeptide chains and control most of the activities of cells and organisms. For example, **enzymes** allow chemical reactions to occur fast enough for life, and **antibodies** make the immune system effective; without them many processes would fail. Polypeptides (and the proteins they form) are therefore essential for the structure and function of cells and whole organisms.

questions.question:
Achondroplasia is a type of dwarfism present in humans, characterised by shortened limbs. The trait has an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. The pedigree shows the inheritance of this genetic disorder.

Explain why the inheritance pattern of achondroplasia is autosomal, as opposed to sex-linked, with reference to individuals from the 1st and 2nd generation.
questions.answer:
If the trait were X-linked dominant, the affected father ($X^AY$) would pass his $X^A$ to **all** his daughters, so none of the daughters in the 2nd generation could be unaffected. But the pedigree shows unaffected daughters, so it is not X-linked. (If Y-linked, an unaffected son could not occur, as every son inherits the father's Y.)

If the trait were X-linked recessive ($X^aY \times X^aX^a$), all sons would be affected and all daughters unaffected, which does not match the pedigree. So the trait must be **autosomal**.

questions.question:
Achondroplasia is a type of dwarfism present in humans, characterised by shortened limbs. The trait has an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. The pedigree shows the inheritance of this genetic disorder.

Predict the likelihood that individuals labelled I and II will bear a child with achondroplasia. Show your working.
questions.answer:
Individual I is affected, but his mother was unaffected ($aa$), so I is heterozygous **Aa**. Individual II is unaffected: **aa**.

| | $a$ | $a$ |
|---|---|---|
| $A$ | $Aa$ | $Aa$ |
| $a$ | $aa$ | $aa$ |

There is a **50%** chance that a child will have achondroplasia ($Aa$).

questions.question:
DNA profiling (DNA fingerprint analysis) is used to identify and compare individuals based on similarities and differences in their DNA. The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is one technique used in this process.

Describe how the polymerase chain reaction is carried out and outline its role in the process of DNA profiling.
questions.answer:
PCR copies (amplifies) DNA. The DNA is **heated** to separate it into single strands. Primers, free nucleotides and DNA polymerase are added and the mixture is **cooled** so primers bind to the single strands. Polymerase then joins free nucleotides to each strand to form two copies of the original DNA. The cycle repeats, so the amount of DNA doubles with each cycle.

In DNA profiling, PCR increases the amount of DNA from a very small sample so there is enough to cut with restriction enzymes and run on a gel to produce the profile.

questions.question: Draw a flow chart to outline what happens in the inflammatory response.
questions.answer: Pathogen enters the body through a wound (e.g. cut) $\to$ damaged cells and mast cells release **histamine** $\to$ blood vessels dilate (vasodilation) and become more permeable $\to$ increased blood flow and fluid/plasma leak into the tissue (redness, heat, swelling) $\to$ phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages) move to the site and engulf pathogens $\to$ pathogens destroyed and tissue repaired.

questions.question:
Researchers are investigating viral antigen-producing genes that rarely mutate as a step in developing a universal flu vaccine. If successful, this advance could reduce the need for yearly flu vaccinations as new flu strains arise.

Use your knowledge of the immune system to explain how this could be a successful approach in the prevention of influenza outbreaks.
questions.answer:
A vaccine introduces weakened or dead pathogen particles or antigens so the immune system makes a primary response and forms **memory B and T cells**. On later exposure these give a faster, stronger secondary response.

The immune response is **specific**: a vaccine protects only if the antigen on the pathogen matches the antigen used in the vaccine. If the viral antigens mutate, the vaccine no longer protects, so a new vaccine is needed each year. A vaccine based on regions of viral proteins that rarely mutate would stay matched to the virus despite mutations elsewhere, so one vaccine could continue to protect against new strains.

questions.question:
City A is experiencing an epidemic of a previously unknown infectious disease, X. Doctors believe Disease X is spread through direct contact and is most likely caused by Bacteria Y.

Using your knowledge of Koch's postulates, outline an experiment to establish Bacteria Y as the cause of Disease X. Include a risk assessment in your answer.
questions.answer:
1. Show that Bacteria Y is present in all organisms with Disease X (e.g. by microscopy and culturing samples on agar plates).
2. Isolate Bacteria Y from a patient and grow it in pure culture in the lab.
3. Inoculate a pure sample of Bacteria Y into a healthy host and check that the same symptoms of Disease X appear.
4. Re-isolate Bacteria Y from the second host and identify it as the same bacterium.
5. Repeat the experiment (e.g. 10 times) for reliability.

| Risk | Precaution |
|---|---|
| Infection of the technician | Wear a mask, gloves and other PPE when handling biohazard material; autoclave all materials after testing |
| Lab contamination / outbreak of the disease | Work in a biosafety cabinet or fume hood; sterilise surfaces and equipment after use |

questions.question:
Some pathogens require a vector in order to infect a new host.

Outline an example of an infectious disease that is caused by a vector-transmitted pathogen. Name both the pathogen and the vector in your answer.
questions.answer: **Malaria** is caused by the protozoan ***Plasmodium*** (pathogen) and is carried by the ***Anopheles* mosquito** (vector).

questions.question:
Some pathogens require a vector in order to infect a new host.

Outline an adaptive feature of either the vector or the pathogen that facilitates transmission of the disease.
questions.answer: The *Plasmodium* parasite infects the **salivary glands** of the mosquito, so it is passed on easily to a new host when the mosquito takes a blood meal.

questions.question:
Some pathogens require a vector in order to infect a new host.

Discuss preventative measures that have been successfully used to combat the disease.
questions.answer: **Draining swamps** where mosquitoes breed, and using **insecticides** to kill adult mosquitoes, reduce the number of vectors and so reduce transmission. (Releasing genetically engineered sterile mosquitoes, or mosquitoes that impair *Plasmodium* development, is also acceptable.)

questions.question:
Plants carry out photosynthesis during daylight hours, using carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) from the atmosphere that enters the leaves through the stomata. In most plants, called C3 plants, the $\text{CO}_2$ cannot be stored and is immediately converted to glucose through a complex series of biochemical reactions. Some plants, however, can capture $\text{CO}_2$ at night and use it during the day. These are called CAM plants. The terms C3 and CAM refer to specific compounds involved in their respective photosynthetic reactions.

The following graphs show the stomatal conductance (the degree of stomatal opening) over a 24-hour period in representative C3 and CAM plants. The C3 plant is from the ground storey of a rainforest and the CAM plant is a cactus. The black bars on the horizontal axes indicate night-time hours. The two plants are illustrated below the graphs.

Use the information provided to discuss how both structural and physiological features adapt each plant to its environment.
questions.answer:
**C3 plant** (wet, shaded rainforest floor): *Structural:* large, broad green leaves capture as much light as possible. *Physiological:* it cannot store $\text{CO}_2$ at night, so its stomata are open during the day to take in $\text{CO}_2$ for photosynthesis. Water loss by transpiration is not a serious problem in a wet environment.

**CAM plant** (cactus, hot and dry): *Structural:* leaves reduced to spines reduce the surface area for water loss. *Physiological:* stomata open at night and stay closed for most of the day, reducing transpiration; the $\text{CO}_2$ taken in at night is stored and used for photosynthesis during the day.

questions.question:
A group of students carried out a practical investigation to grow and identify the bacteria in yoghurt. After examining a range of secondary sources, they hypothesised that they would find a species of *Lactobacillus*.

They set up four agar plates with a basic nutrient agar, sterilised their inoculating loop and applied yoghurt to three of the plates. One plate received no yoghurt as a control. Plates were then placed into an incubator at 23 degrees Celsius for five days. The colour, shape and profile of any bacterial colonies formed were then observed and compared with established data on *Lactobacillus* species. They obtained the following results.

| Plate | Number of colonies matching *Lactobacillus* description | Number of colonies not consistent with *Lactobacillus* description |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 13 | 10 |
| 2 | 20 | 15 |
| 3 | 15 | 25 |
| Control | 0 | 5 |

What conclusion can be made from this data?
questions.answer: *Lactobacillus* species appear to be present (some evidence supports the hypothesis), but the control plate grew colonies, so **contamination** has occurred and the results are not valid without improvements to the method.

questions.question:
A group of students carried out a practical investigation to grow and identify the bacteria in yoghurt. After examining a range of secondary sources, they hypothesised that they would find a species of *Lactobacillus*.

They set up four agar plates with a basic nutrient agar, sterilised their inoculating loop and applied yoghurt to three of the plates. One plate received no yoghurt as a control. Plates were then placed into an incubator at 23 degrees Celsius for five days. The colour, shape and profile of any bacterial colonies formed were then observed and compared with established data on *Lactobacillus* species. They obtained the following results.

| Plate | Number of colonies matching *Lactobacillus* description | Number of colonies not consistent with *Lactobacillus* description |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 13 | 10 |
| 2 | 20 | 15 |
| 3 | 15 | 25 |
| Control | 0 | 5 |

Explain TWO improvements that should be made to the students' experiment.
questions.answer:
1. **Replicate** both the treatments and the controls (more plates). Results can then be averaged, so outliers do not lead to incorrect conclusions (reliability).
2. **Improve handling of the agar plates** (aseptic technique): keep plates closed until immediately before the sample is applied, hold them vertically while streaking so airborne microbes do not land on the agar, seal them straight after streaking, and avoid breathing on the plates or touching the agar. This prevents contamination, such as the growth seen on the control plate (validity).

(Controlling variables such as the amount of agar and of yoghurt, and using the same yoghurt, would also improve validity.)

questions.question:
Recent advances in biotechnology, particularly the production of recombinant DNA, have provided increasingly powerful tools for the diagnosis, prevention and treatment of various diseases.

Describe the process to produce recombinant DNA.
questions.answer:
DNA containing the target gene is isolated and cut out using a **restriction enzyme**, which leaves sticky ends. A bacterial **plasmid** is cut with the same restriction enzyme so it has complementary sticky ends. The target gene binds to the plasmid by complementary base pairing of the sticky ends, and **DNA ligase** bonds the sugar-phosphate backbones. The recombinant plasmid is taken up by a bacterium, which replicates and so amplifies the target DNA.

(Alternatively: in CRISPR-Cas9, a guide RNA complementary to the target sequence directs the Cas9 enzyme to cut the DNA, and the desired gene is inserted.)

questions.question:
Recent advances in biotechnology, particularly the production of recombinant DNA, have provided increasingly powerful tools for the diagnosis, prevention and treatment of various diseases.

Using specific examples, justify the use of genetic technologies in medicine for the prevention or treatment of at least one infectious and at least one non-infectious disease.
questions.answer:
**Infectious disease: COVID-19 or influenza.** Plasmids or mRNA engineered to carry the code for a viral antigen are used as vaccines. The recipient's own cells make the antigen, which stimulates the immune system and produces immune memory. This is justified because once the genetic makeup of the pathogen is known, a DNA or mRNA vaccine can be made easily and very quickly, and antigen production inside the recipient's cells leads to efficient generation of cytotoxic and helper T cells.

**Non-infectious disease: diabetes.** Diabetes occurs when the pancreas does not make enough insulin or the body cannot use it effectively. Insulin used to be taken from the pancreas of slaughtered pigs and cattle, which differs slightly in amino acid sequence from human insulin and contains impurities, so some patients had allergic reactions. Now the human insulin gene is inserted into the plasmid of a bacterium, which produces large amounts of pure human insulin that can be extracted for use. This is justified because it is cheaper, more plentiful, and safer than animal-sourced insulin.

questions.question:
The graph and table below show data describing the COVID-19 pandemic (graph: NSW COVID-19 cases over time).

**NSW COVID vaccination rate, updated March 2022**

| | Total (ages 16 and over) | Total (ages 12-15) | Total (ages 5-11) |
|---|---|---|---|
| All providers - first dose | 95.8% | 83.6% | 47.9% |
| All providers - second dose | 94.4% | 79.0% | 1.7% |
| All providers - third dose | 55.8% | X | X |

With reference to the above data and information, discuss the role of public health campaigns in keeping people safe during the COVID-19 pandemic.
questions.answer:
Public health campaigns inform people about health dangers and how to avoid them, e.g. advertising encouraging social distancing, mask wearing and vaccination.

The **graph** shows that after an initial rise in cases (about 2000 cases in March 2020), cases fell in the following months (about 1000 in April and below 200 in May), suggesting government interventions had a positive effect. However, cases rose again later in 2020 (about 400-500 in July), showing campaigns are not always fully successful and must be re-evaluated using epidemiological data.

The **table** shows high vaccination uptake in people aged 16 and over (95.8% first dose, 94.4% second dose, 55.8% third dose), suggesting people followed the health advice. Uptake was much lower in the 5-11 age group (47.9% first dose, 1.7% second dose), so campaigns were less effective, or had been running for less time, for that group.

questions.question:
"Advances in reproductive and genetic technologies have allowed humans to manipulate the gene pools of both domesticated and wild populations of plants and animals. There are concerns, however, that the results of these technologies may also harm ecosystems and lead to a decrease in biodiversity."

Evaluate these statements with reference to specific examples.
questions.answer:
**Reproductive technologies**, such as artificial pollination and artificial insemination, allow rapid, economical selective breeding of plants and animals with desired traits (e.g. disease resistance, high-quality milk or meat). Whole-animal cloning (transferring the nucleus of a somatic cell into an enucleated egg and implanting the embryo in a surrogate) produces copies of animals with desirable characteristics.

**Genetic technologies** such as transgenic crops (e.g. Roundup Ready soy, Bt cotton) are made by inserting genes using plasmid or viral vectors or microinjection into egg cells, giving herbicide or pest resistance. Genome sequencing can also guide captive breeding of wild species such as the northern quoll.

**Evaluation:** The statements are largely supported. Cloning and selective breeding produce populations with very similar or identical genomes, reducing genetic diversity, so a single pathogen or environmental change could wipe out whole populations. If transgenic varieties are grown exclusively, traditional and heritage varieties can disappear. Genes from engineered plants (e.g. herbicide resistance) may transfer by pollen to wild relatives or weeds, creating weeds that are hard to control, and Bt crops could harm non-target native insects. Antibiotic-resistance marker genes could also escape and produce resistant pathogens. Against this, Bt crops can reduce pesticide use, which benefits non-target insects, and technologies used in conservation (captive breeding guided by genome data) can protect genetic diversity. Overall, the technologies have a real potential to harm biodiversity, but the outcome depends on how they are managed.

questions.question:
Prions and viruses are both non-cellular pathogens. Which row of the table correctly identifies the characteristics of viruses and prions?

| | Prion | Virus |
|---|---|---|
| (A) | eukaryotic | prokaryotic |
| (B) | chain of amino acids that has folded into an incorrect form | chain of nucleotides |
| (C) | chain of polypeptides folded correctly | bases that have folded incorrectly |
| (D) | macroscopic | microscopic |
questions.answer: A prion is a protein (a chain of amino acids) that has misfolded; a virus is a nucleic acid (a chain of nucleotides) in a protein coat. Neither is a cell, so neither is prokaryotic or eukaryotic, and both are microscopic.
options: Row A
Row B
Row C
Row D

questions.question: Robert Koch developed postulates for disease. Which of the following statements best describes the purpose of Koch's postulates?
questions.answer: Koch's postulates are a set of steps for showing that a particular microorganism is the cause of a particular disease.
options: The microorganism that causes a specific disease can be identified.
Healthy organisms can become sick when infected with a microorganism.
Microbes from the air were wrapped in glass tubing during Koch's famous experiments.
Cultures of a disease-causing pathogen can always be grown from samples of unhealthy animals.

questions.question: What are the features of passive immunity?
questions.answer: In passive immunity the person receives ready-made antibodies (e.g. across the placenta or in breast milk). The person's own immune system is not activated, so no memory cells form and no antibodies are produced by the person, and the protection is short-lived as the antibodies break down.
options: A long-term effective period, memory cells and antibodies produced.
A short-term effective period, memory cells and antibodies produced.
A long-term effective period, no memory cells and no antibodies produced.
A short-term effective period, no memory cells and no antibodies produced.

questions.question: Which response identifies two chemical barriers to the transmission of pathogens?
questions.answer: Stomach acid (low pH) and tears (which contain the enzyme lysozyme) are chemical barriers. Skin and cilia are physical barriers, and white blood cells are part of the cellular response.
options: Skin and urine.
Stomach acid and tears.
Mucus and white blood cells.
Stomach acid and cilia in the respiratory tract.

questions.question: Bush medicine is an exciting area of disease treatment because:
questions.answer: Many native plants contain compounds with antimicrobial or other medicinal properties that may be developed into treatments. The other options are wrong: native plants can be toxic, Aboriginal intellectual property rights must be respected, and any treatment needs rigorous testing.
options: There is little risk when using native plants.
Intellectual property is not a consideration when exploiting these plants.
There is little need for rigorous scientific testing before their use in patients.
Some properties of plants may be useful in managing modern infectious diseases.

questions.question: A germ-line mutation is one which:
questions.answer: Germ-line mutations occur in cells that form gametes (sex cells), so they can be passed on to offspring. Mutations in somatic (body) cells cannot.
options: affects sex cells.
affects somatic cells.
is acquired from a virus.
changes the virulence of a pathogen.

questions.question:
In order to investigate the microbes present in a range of water samples, a group of students carried out the following procedure:
1. 12 identical agar plates were made in sterile petri dishes.
2. Samples of tap water, rain water and dam water were collected.
3. 3 agar plates were sealed.
4. An inoculation loop was heated in a Bunsen burner flame, cooled, inserted into the tap water sample then swiped over the surface of one of the remaining agar plates.
5. The agar plate was then sealed.
6. Steps 4–5 were repeated twice.
7. Steps 4–6 were repeated with the rain water sample and then the dam water sample.
8. All plates were incubated for 3 days at $35^\circ$C.
9. Each plate was observed, and the number, appearance, size and shape of each colony was recorded.
10. The agar plates were heated and then disposed of.

Which response correctly identifies the purpose of the step outlined?
questions.answer: Using identical plates keeps every variable other than the water source the same, so any differences in colonies can be attributed to the water source: this supports validity. Step 4 (flaming the loop) is aseptic technique, not reliability (repeating in step 6 gives reliability); step 3 gives a sealed control plate; and step 10, not step 8, is the safety step.
options: Step 1 is important for ensuring validity.
Step 4 is important for ensuring reliability.
Step 3 is important for ensuring variables are controlled.
Step 8 is important for ensuring a safe working environment.

questions.question: Rickets is a disease that is caused by a mutation on the X chromosome. It can be passed on to offspring. What type of disease is rickets?
questions.answer: A disease caused by a mutation that can be inherited is a genetic disease. (Rickets in the question is the X-linked form.)
options: Cancer.
Genetic.
Nutritional.
Environmental.

questions.question: External fertilisation:
questions.answer: External fertilisation needs water for sperm to swim to the eggs and to stop the gametes drying out, so it occurs in aquatic environments. It produces large numbers of gametes and little parental care.
options: mainly occurs in terrestrial animals.
only occurs in aquatic environments.
involves a small number of female gametes produced.
involves a great deal of parental care for subsequent offspring.

questions.question:
Consider the following definition.

*It makes up over 90% of the human genome, most of it lies between genes on the chromosomes and it has few known functions.*

Which of the following is referred to by the definition?
questions.answer: Non-coding DNA makes up most of the genome (over 90% in humans) and lies between genes; much of it has no known function.
options: Coding DNA
Autosomal DNA
Non-coding DNA
Messenger RNA (mRNA)

questions.question:
Endotherms possess adaptations to maintain their body temperature within tolerable limits. Adaptations can be behavioural, structural and physiological. The following are adaptations of endotherms to a hot environment.

i. Counter-current heat exchange to increase heat loss from extremities
ii. Decreased metabolic rate to reduce the amount of heat produced
iii. Vasodilation of blood vessels to increase heat loss by radiation
iv. Sweating to increase heat lost from skin
v. Move into the shade

Which of the following responses correctly classifies the type of adaptation shown by the options identified?

| | Adaptation | Type of adaptation |
|---|---|---|
| (A) | ii, iii, iv | Physiological |
| (B) | ii, iv, v | Behavioural |
| (C) | ii, iv | Structural |
| (D) | i, v | Physiological |
questions.answer: Changing metabolic rate (ii), vasodilation (iii) and sweating (iv) are all physiological processes. Moving into the shade (v) is behavioural, and counter-current exchange (i) is structural, so rows B, C and D are wrong.
options: Row A
Row B
Row C
Row D

questions.question: Governments invest in education programs to reduce the incidence of childhood obesity, as a rise in childhood obesity has been linked to higher rates of type 2 diabetes in children. The purpose of these education programs is to:
questions.answer: Education programs are a prevention strategy: they aim to stop obesity (and so type 2 diabetes) developing in the first place.
options: Prevent the occurrence of obesity.
Cure children with type 2 diabetes.
Make children aware of the treatments for diabetes.
Prevent discrimination against children who are overweight or obese.

questions.question: The diagram below represents which of the following types of epidemiological studies?
questions.answer: The diagram compares the medical histories of patients who already have the disease (cases) with those of healthy control subjects, looking backwards to find a link with a possible cause. That is a case-control study.
options: Cohort study.
Descriptive study.
Intervention study.
Case-control study.

questions.question:
The following graph shows the leading causes of death in Australia between 2007 and 2016. Use this graph to answer the question.

What is the death rate per 100 000 population for ischaemic heart diseases in 2016?
questions.answer: The top (ischaemic heart disease) line is at about 62 in 2016.

questions.question:
The following graph shows the leading causes of death in Australia between 2007 and 2016. Use this graph to answer the question.

Which of the following is the best description of the trend shown on the graph for the death rate per 100 000 from 2007–2016 for cerebrovascular diseases?
questions.answer: The cerebrovascular line (grey) is at about 50 in 2007 and 2008, then declines steadily to about 35 by 2016. Option D describes ischaemic heart disease.
options: Decreases from 50 per 100 000 in 2007 to 35 per 100 000 in 2016.
Shows a very gradual decrease from 34 per 100 000 in 2007 to 30 per 100 000 in 2016.
Remains constant at 50 per 100 000 in 2007 and 2008, after which it decreases at a generally constant rate until it reaches 35 per 100 000 in 2016.
Remains constant at 100 per 100 000 in 2007 and 2008, after which it decreases at a generally constant rate until it reaches 62 per 100 000 in 2016.

questions.question: The Australian Budgerigar is a small Australian parrot which has 26 chromosomes in a general body cell. One easy way for the vet to determine a bird's gender is to analyse the bird's DNA using a PCR-based test. This test identifies a bird's gender based on its chromosome pair (ZW in females and ZZ in males). What is the total number of autosomes that occur in a general body cell in a female budgerigar?
questions.answer: A body cell has 26 chromosomes, of which 2 are sex chromosomes (Z and W). The other $26 - 2 = 24$ are autosomes.

questions.question:
The table shows the changes in the human body when an individual begins exercising: the rate of cellular respiration increases, the concentration of carbon dioxide in the blood increases, the concentration of oxygen in the blood decreases, the pH of blood decreases and the rate of breathing increases.

The following steps are processes in the stimulus–response pathway.
I. Nerves send a signal to an effector.
II. Chemoreceptors detect a decrease in blood pH.
III. Nerves send a signal about lower blood pH to the brain.
IV. Muscles in the pulmonary system (diaphragm) contract and relax at a faster rate, returning oxygen and carbon dioxide to optimum levels.

What is the correct order of steps to explain the changes in the human body when an individual begins exercising?
questions.answer: Stimulus-response pathway: receptor detects the change (II) $\to$ sensory nerves carry the message to the brain/control centre (III) $\to$ motor nerves send a signal to the effector (I) $\to$ effector muscles respond (IV).
options: II, IV, I, III.
I, II, III, IV.
II, III, I, IV.
II, I, IV, III.

questions.question: Which of the following describes DNA polymerase? An enzyme that:
questions.answer: DNA polymerase adds free nucleotides to the growing new strand, using the original strand as a template. Restriction enzymes splice DNA, ligase joins fragments and helicase uncoils the DNA.
options: splices DNA at specific recognition sites.
adds nucleotides to a newly forming DNA strand.
joins together fragments of newly synthesised DNA.
uncoils DNA by breaking the hydrogen bond between base pairs.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of how the environment might affect the expression of a gene in an individual?
questions.answer: Temperature (an environmental factor) changes whether the pigment gene is expressed in the Himalayan rabbit's fur. Option D is incomplete dominance, and B and A are not examples of the environment changing gene expression.
options: Many people with red hair also have freckles and green eyes.
Identical twins brought up in different areas show many physical similarities.
Black fur develops under a cold pack placed on the white fur of a Himalayan rabbit.
Homozygous snapdragon plants have red or white flowers, but hybrids have pink flowers.

questions.question:
Which of the following correctly identifies the reproduction methods of the different organisms?

| | Fungi | Bacteria | Protists |
|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | Budding and spores | Binary fission only | Binary fission |
| (B) | Spores only | Binary fission only | Binary fission and budding |
| (C) | Binary fission only | Spores only | Budding and spores |
| (D) | Binary fission and budding | Budding and spores | Spores only |
questions.answer: Fungi reproduce by budding (yeasts) and spores, bacteria by binary fission, and protists by binary fission (budding is also listed for protists in the syllabus, but row A is the only row with the correct fungi and bacteria entries).
options: Row A
Row B
Row C
Row D

questions.question:
Proteins are the most abundant organic compound in organisms, formed through the process of polypeptide synthesis.

Describe the process of translation in polypeptide synthesis.
questions.answer: Translation takes place at a ribosome in the cytoplasm. The mRNA, made in transcription, moves through the ribosome. Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry specific amino acids to the ribosome. The tRNA anticodon pairs with the complementary codon on the mRNA, so the amino acids are placed in the order the mRNA specifies and are joined by peptide bonds to form a chain (a polypeptide). When a stop codon is reached the polypeptide is released.

questions.question:
Proteins are the most abundant organic compound in organisms, formed through the process of polypeptide synthesis.

Justify this statement using TWO specific named examples of proteins you have studied in this subject.

*"It is essential that the correct proteins are synthesised to maintain structure and function in the human body."*
questions.answer:
The statement is justified: if the wrong protein is made, a body function fails. Two examples:

- **Helicase (an enzyme):** it unwinds the DNA double helix at the start of DNA replication, which is needed in mitosis and meiosis. If helicase were faulty, DNA could not be copied, so cells could not replicate, which would stop growth and repair.
- **Insulin (a hormone):** it is released by the pancreas when blood glucose rises, and it helps body cells take up glucose and convert it to glycogen, lowering blood glucose. Correctly made insulin is essential for homeostasis of blood glucose and for supplying cells with glucose for respiration; a faulty insulin protein leads to disease (diabetes).

Both show that the structure of a protein determines its function, so correct synthesis is essential.

questions.question:
Huntington's Disease (HD) is an autosomal genetic condition. Matt and his wife Ella do not have the disease but are concerned that their daughter Leah may be affected. Both of Matt's parents and his brother Bill all have Huntington's disease.

Using the information provided, draw a pedigree for this family.
questions.answer:
A correct pedigree (squares are males, circles are females, shaded symbols have Huntington's disease):
- **Generation I:** Matt's father (shaded square) and Matt's mother (shaded circle), joined by a marriage line.
- **Generation II:** their two sons, Matt (unshaded square) and Bill (shaded square), joined to the parents by a descent line. Matt is joined by a marriage line to Ella (unshaded circle).
- **Generation III:** Matt and Ella's daughter Leah (circle; unknown, since it is not known if she is affected).
- **Key:** shaded = has HD, unshaded = unaffected.

questions.question:
Huntington's Disease (HD) is an autosomal genetic condition. Matt and his wife Ella do not have the disease but are concerned that their daughter Leah may be affected. Both of Matt's parents and his brother Bill all have Huntington's disease.

Determine whether Huntington's disease is caused by a dominant or recessive allele. Justify your answer using the pedigree.
questions.answer: HD is caused by a **dominant** allele. In the pedigree, both of Matt's parents (generation I) have HD, but their son Matt does not. Two affected parents can only have an unaffected child if both parents are heterozygous and the unaffected child is homozygous recessive. If HD were recessive, both parents would be homozygous recessive and all their children would have HD, including Matt.

questions.question:
Huntington's Disease (HD) is an autosomal genetic condition. Matt and his wife Ella do not have the disease but are concerned that their daughter Leah may be affected. Both of Matt's parents and his brother Bill all have Huntington's disease.

Bill is heterozygous and marries a woman who does not have Huntington's disease. Use a Punnett square to determine the genotypic ratio of any future children they may have.
questions.answer:
Key: $H$ = Huntington's disease allele (dominant), $h$ = normal allele.

Bill is $Hh$ and the woman, who does not have HD, is $hh$.

| | $h$ | $h$ |
|---|---|---|
| $H$ | $Hh$ | $Hh$ |
| $h$ | $hh$ | $hh$ |

Genotypic ratio: **1 $Hh$ : 1 $hh$** (50% $Hh$, 50% $hh$).

questions.question:
Diagram 1 shows the levels of two hormones released from the ovaries and two hormones released from the pituitary gland over a menstrual cycle. The ovarian hormones are W (blue line) and X (orange line); the pituitary hormones are Y (before ovulation) and Z (peaking at ovulation).

Identify ONE of the hormones W, X, Y or Z and explain the changes in levels of this hormone over the menstrual cycle.
questions.answer:
**W is oestrogen.** Oestrogen is released from the ovary in response to FSH and LH, which cause the follicles to develop. Its level rises to a surge just before ovulation (around day 12–13), then drops after ovulation, with a smaller second rise as the corpus luteum releases it to build up the lining of the uterus. The level drops again just before menstruation as the corpus luteum breaks down.

(Alternatively, **X is progesterone**: it is released by the corpus luteum after ovulation, rising to maintain the uterine lining, then falls just before menstruation as the corpus luteum disintegrates. **Y is FSH**, which stimulates follicle development early in the cycle and is suppressed after ovulation. **Z is LH**, which surges at ovulation, triggered by the oestrogen peak.)

questions.question:
Diagram 2 shows the menstrual cycle of a woman during the month of January: menstruation on 2–6 January and again on 29–31 January, and ovulation on 15 January.

Using the graphs in Diagram 1, state which date in January her oestrogen levels will be at their highest?
questions.answer: In Diagram 1, oestrogen peaks about three days before ovulation. Ovulation is on 15 January, so oestrogen is highest on about **12 January** (11–13 January accepted).

questions.question:
*"Ring a ring o' roses, A pocket full of posies. Atishoo! Atishoo! We all fall down."*

This children's rhyme originated as a description of the Black Death, the plague that killed some 40% of the population during the 14th century. The 'pocket full of posies' refers to the pomanders of sweet smelling herbs that people carried or wore around their neck to ward off the bad air that they believed caused the disease. We now know that the plague is caused by the bacterium *Yersinia pestis* carried in the gut of biting fleas on rodents (primarily rats).

With reference to the information above and your knowledge of disease transmission, evaluate the effectiveness of the pomander in controlling this plague.
questions.answer: The pomander was **ineffective**. People believed the stimulus was bad air (miasma), but the plague is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium *Yersinia pestis*, not by bad air. Sweet-smelling herbs neither stop the pathogen entering the body nor destroy it. The bacterium was transmitted when a rat flea (the vector) bit a person and delivered bacteria from its gut into the bite, so the pomander does nothing to prevent fleas biting. Control would have needed measures such as controlling rats and fleas, hygiene and quarantine.

questions.question:
Varroa mites (*Varroa destructor* and *Varroa jacobsoni*) are parasites that feed on adult honey bees and their larvae. They weaken and kill honey bee colonies and can also transmit honey bee viruses such as deformed wing virus, which affects bees' ability to fly.

Varroa mites were detected in biosecurity surveillance hives in Newcastle in late June 2022 and in hives on the Central Coast of NSW within a few days of this finding. The pest affects every other major beekeeping area in the world. Concerns have been raised about it becoming established in Australia.

Outline TWO methods that could be used to prevent the spread of varroa mite within Australia.
questions.answer:
1. **Destroy infected hives:** infected hives are destroyed immediately, together with all hives (even uninfected ones) within a set eradication zone, to remove the mite and stop it spreading.
2. **Restrict movement (quarantine):** no hives, bees or beekeeping equipment may be moved out of the eradication zone, and equipment from the zone must be burnt or fumigated, so mites are not carried to other areas.

(Other accepted methods: hives cannot be re-established in the area for a set time; sterilising clothes and equipment used with infected hives.)

questions.question:
Varroa mites (*Varroa destructor* and *Varroa jacobsoni*) are parasites that feed on adult honey bees and their larvae. They weaken and kill honey bee colonies and can also transmit honey bee viruses such as deformed wing virus, which affects bees' ability to fly. Varroa mites were detected in NSW in June 2022. The pest affects every other major beekeeping area in the world.

Assess the potential impacts of the varroa mite on agricultural production in Australia.
questions.answer:
The varroa mite will have a **very significant negative impact** on agricultural production in Australia if it becomes established.

- **Honey and bee products:** the mite feeds on adult bees and their larvae and can destroy whole colonies, and all hives in a large eradication zone must be destroyed. This reduces the production of honey and bee-related products such as beeswax and royal jelly (used in medicinal products).
- **Pollinated crops:** bees pollinate crops such as fruit trees (e.g. almonds, apples). The destruction of hives, plus viral diseases such as deformed wing virus transmitted by the mites that stop bees flying, would reduce pollination and so the yield of fruit and other crops.

Overall, the impact is severe because production of honey and many pollinated crops would fall.

questions.question:
Monkeypox is a rare disease caused by infection with the monkeypox virus. Monkeypox virus belongs to the *Orthopoxvirus* genus. The *Orthopoxvirus* genus also includes variola virus (which causes smallpox), vaccinia virus (used in the smallpox vaccine), and cowpox virus. Monkeypox is not related to chickenpox.

**Multi-country monkeypox outbreak: situation update from the World Health Organisation (WHO), 27 June 2022**
This Disease Outbreak News on the current monkeypox outbreak is an update to the previously published editions. It is based on outcomes of the International Health Regulations Emergency Committee regarding the multi-country monkeypox outbreak held on 23 June.

*Outbreak at a glance:* Since 1 January and as of 22 June 2022, 3413 laboratory confirmed cases and one death have been reported to WHO from 50 countries/territories in five WHO Regions. In the period 17 June to 22 June, 1310 new cases have been reported and eight new countries have reported cases. The majority of laboratory confirmed cases (86%) were reported from the WHO European Region.

The figure below shows the geographic distribution of confirmed cases of monkeypox reported to or identified by WHO from official public sources, 1 January to 22 June 2022.

Evaluate the validity and accuracy of the data provided in the article.
questions.answer:
The data is **both valid and accurate**.

- **Valid:** the information is provided by the World Health Organisation, a highly reputable source, and directly addresses the outbreak of monkeypox virus. It is up to date and based on the outcomes of the International Health Regulations Emergency Committee meeting specifically about this outbreak.
- **Accurate:** the cases reported are laboratory confirmed, and were identified by WHO or reported to WHO from official public sources, so they are reliable. The data is also dated (22 June 2022) and gives numbers and percentages for the total and recent cases that are matched by the map.

(A limitation: the map only shows confirmed cases, so countries with limited testing may be under-reported.)

questions.question:
Monkeypox is a rare disease caused by infection with the monkeypox virus.

Tecovirimat is an antiviral drug with recent regulatory approval from the European Medicines Agency for orthopoxvirus-associated infections, including monkeypox. Describe how this drug may be helpful in treating patients with monkeypox.
questions.answer: Antiviral drugs do not kill viruses. Tecovirimat may slow the progress of monkeypox by preventing the virus from invading (spreading to) other cells and reproducing inside infected cells, which gives the immune system time to take over and destroy the pathogen.

questions.question:
Monkeypox is a rare disease caused by infection with the monkeypox virus, which belongs to the *Orthopoxvirus* genus along with the variola (smallpox), vaccinia and cowpox viruses.

Vaccines made from the variola and vaccinia viruses are also effective against monkeypox virus. Explain how these vaccines provide immunity against this disease.
questions.answer: A vaccine contains an antigen (a weakened or related virus) which triggers a specific immune response from B and T lymphocytes that match the antigen. Once the antigen has been destroyed, memory B and T cells for that antigen remain, giving **active immunity**: if the antigen is met again, the response is faster and stronger. The variola and vaccinia viruses and the monkeypox virus are closely related (all orthopoxviruses), so they carry the same or very similar antigens. The memory cells made after the vaccine therefore recognise and respond rapidly to the monkeypox virus.

questions.question:
You are an ophthalmologist (eye specialist) who has had a visit from a 25-year-old patient. She is an avid netball player and reader. She is having trouble viewing text on her laptop and in books, describing the letters as looking blurry.

Identify the condition she has and describe the causes.

You are an ophthalmologist (eye specialist) who has had a visit from a 25-year-old patient. She is an avid netball player and reader. She is having trouble viewing text on her laptop and in books, describing the letters as looking blurry (she has hyperopia).

In a table, discuss the TWO best treatment options available to this patient that will assist with this vision impairment.
questions.answer:
Contact lenses and laser eye surgery (LASIK) suit an active person; glasses are not the best option as she plays netball.

| Technology | Description | Positives | Negatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Contact lenses** | A convex lens is placed on the cornea, shaped to suit the curvature of the eyeball. It increases the refraction (bending) of light so near objects focus on the retina and are seen clearly. | Corrects vision reliably. Does not change her appearance. Can be worn easily for netball games. | Can reduce the cleansing effect of tears and cause dry or uncomfortable eyes. Blood vessels may swell. Must be carefully cleaned and sterilised to avoid infection. |
| **LASIK (laser eye surgery)** | A flap of the cornea is cut and lifted. A laser reshapes the middle layers of the cornea to increase its curvature and so its refractive power, then the flap is replaced. Light is bent more so it lands on the retina, giving a clear image. | Vision is corrected, so no glasses or contacts are needed. Lasts up to 20 years. Quick, painless procedure. Good for active people. | Expensive. Invasive, with a risk of eye infection or damage. About a week of recovery and may cause dry eyes. She may need glasses again in future as vision changes with age (long-sightedness). |

Both correct her hyperopia; contact lenses are cheaper and reversible, while LASIK is a long-term solution.

questions.question:
Read the information in the storyboard: a seal colony is attacked by a killer whale ("Dinner!"), the seals say "This is not good" and "Time to find a safer location", and some of the seals move to an iceberg and establish a new population.

Identify the process occurring in the storyboard and describe the effect on the future gene pool of the new seal population.
questions.answer: The process is **genetic drift, specifically the founder effect**: a small group leaves the original population and founds a new one. The new population is small, so its members carry only some of the alleles of the original population. The new gene pool will therefore have **reduced genetic diversity** (a reduced variety of alleles) and the allele frequencies will differ from the original population's, purely by chance.

questions.question:
A link between high levels of cholesterol in the blood and coronary heart disease has long been recognised by doctors. The Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study followed a group of 4444 people with high levels of blood cholesterol who were all on cholesterol lowering diets. The patients were randomly divided into two equal sized groups. One group was treated with a medication containing the cholesterol lowering drug simvastatin, while the other received a placebo, an identical tablet but without simvastatin. Patients were not aware of which group they were in.

Outline why a placebo group is necessary.
questions.answer: The placebo group is a control group for comparison. It receives an identical tablet without the active ingredient, so any difference in outcome between the groups must be due to whether the subjects took simvastatin, not to other factors (such as the effect of believing they are being treated).

questions.question:
The Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study followed 4444 people with high blood cholesterol (all on cholesterol-lowering diets), divided randomly into two equal groups of 2222: one group was treated with simvastatin and the other received a placebo. The table shows some of the data obtained after six years.

| | Simvastatin Group (SG) (2222 patients) | Placebo Group (PG) (2222 patients) |
|---|---|---|
| Patients who had 1 or more major cardiac events | 431 (19%) | 622 (28%) |
| Patients who died from cardiac arrest (heart attack) | 111 (5%) | 189 (8.5%) |
| Patients who died from non-cardio causes | 46 (2%) | 49 (2.2%) |

Analyse the results shown in the table.
questions.answer:
- **Major cardiac events:** 19% of the simvastatin group had one or more, compared with 28% of the placebo group: the placebo group was about 1.5 times as likely (28/19 $\approx$ 1.5, a 9% difference) to have a major cardiac event.
- **Deaths from cardiac arrest:** 5% (SG) against 8.5% (PG), a 3.5% lower death rate in the simvastatin group, so the placebo group was about 1.7 times as likely to die from a heart attack (8.5/5 = 1.7).
- **Non-cardiac deaths:** 46 vs 49 people (2% vs 2.2%): a very small, insignificant difference, which suggests simvastatin has no other effect on life span.

Overall, simvastatin appears to be an effective drug for preventing cardiac disease and cardiac death.

questions.question:
One factor which can affect blood cholesterol levels is heredity. The *PCSK9* gene found on chromosome 1 codes for a polypeptide which plays a role in the regulation of blood cholesterol levels by cells in the liver. Some alleles of this gene lead to higher blood cholesterol levels and others can lead to lower levels. People with the C679X allele of the gene have much lower cholesterol levels.

The C679X allele is found almost exclusively in African populations. The allele frequency has been found to vary from 0% to 6.9% in populations across West Africa.

Explain TWO processes which may have contributed to the rise of the C679X allele frequency in the European gene pool over the last 50 years.
questions.answer:
1. **Gene flow:** gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations when individuals migrate and interbreed. Migration of people from West Africa (where the allele occurs) to Europe over the last 50 years would have introduced the C679X allele into the European gene pool and, as the migrants breed with Europeans, increased its frequency in the offspring.
2. **Natural selection:** in a population there is variation, with some individuals having C679X and some not. Lower cholesterol reduces the risk of heart disease, which gives the individuals with the allele a survival advantage. They are more likely to survive and reproduce and pass the allele on to their offspring, so the frequency of C679X in the European gene pool increases over generations.

(Genetic drift and mutation are not likely: chance events rarely raise one allele consistently, and mutations are too infrequent to cause such an increase in 50 years.)

questions.question:
Plant species in Australia have adaptations designed to maintain water balance in hot dry conditions. The two maps produced in January 2021 show the highest maximum temperature (Map 1) and the distribution of the major vegetation groups (Map 2).

With reference to the maps, explain how adaptations of Australian plants enable them to survive these hot dry conditions.
questions.answer:
In January 2021, temperatures of up to 42°C and more were experienced across large parts of SA and WA (the brown and red areas of Map 1). Matching these areas with Map 2, the main plant types are **acacias and grasslands** (hummock and tussock grasses), with some eucalypt woodlands and shrublands. These plants survive because of their adaptations for conserving water.

- **Grasses:** leaves are reduced in size or curled (e.g. hummock and tussock grasses). The reduced surface area reduces heat absorption and water lost by transpiration, as there are fewer stomata.
- **Acacias:** the true leaves are very small, and the flattened leaf stalks (phyllodes) photosynthesise but have a small surface area and few stomata, so less water is lost by transpiration.
- **Eucalypts:** leaves hang vertically in hot conditions to reduce the surface area exposed to the sun's rays. Hairs on the surface or sunken stomata trap evaporating water, increasing humidity and limiting transpiration. The shiny waxy cuticle reflects light and reduces the leaf temperature, which reduces evaporative cooling.

The hot dry conditions are a selection pressure: only plants with such adaptations survive and reproduce in these regions, so they dominate the hottest areas.

questions.question:
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare investigated the adequacy of the Australian diet across various life stages to help inform their understanding of nutrition-related health determinants for chronic conditions. Two graphs from their 2018 report are shown: Figure 5.32, the proportion of the population with food group intakes below the recommended serves by sex, aged 14–18 (2011–12), and Figure 5.31, the mean intake of food groups compared with the Australian Dietary Guidelines (ADGs) target, by sex, aged 14–18 (2011–12).

Are diseases caused from incorrect nutrition termed infectious or non-infectious? Why?
questions.answer: **Non-infectious**: diseases caused by a nutritional imbalance are not caused by pathogens and cannot be transmitted from person to person.

questions.question:
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare investigated the adequacy of the Australian diet across various life stages to help inform their understanding of nutrition-related health determinants for chronic conditions. Two graphs from their 2018 report are shown: Figure 5.32, the proportion of the population with food group intakes below the recommended serves by sex, aged 14–18 (2011–12), and Figure 5.31, the mean intake of food groups compared with the Australian Dietary Guidelines (ADGs) target, by sex, aged 14–18 (2011–12).

Draw ONE conclusion from the graphs provided and justify using data.
questions.answer:
**Conclusion:** most Australians aged 14–18 are not eating the recommended serves from the non-discretionary food groups, especially vegetables.

**Justification:** Figure 5.32 shows that about 99% of both boys and girls aged 14–18 have vegetable intakes below the recommended serves. In Figure 5.31, the recommended intake for girls is 5 serves of vegetables per day, but the mean intake is only about 2; for boys the recommended serves is about 5.5, but their mean intake is about 2.2.

questions.question:
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare investigated the adequacy of the Australian diet across various life stages to help inform their understanding of nutrition-related health determinants for chronic conditions. Two graphs from their 2018 report are shown: Figure 5.32, the proportion of the population with food group intakes below the recommended serves by sex, aged 14–18 (2011–12), and Figure 5.31, the mean intake of food groups compared with the Australian Dietary Guidelines (ADGs) target, by sex, aged 14–18 (2011–12).

To obtain the data for these graphs an epidemiological study would have been undertaken. Describe the features of a study that could have produced the data above.

Below are two models that each represent a different aspect of the immune response in humans. Model 1 shows a macrophage engulfing bacteria. Model 2 shows plasma cells releasing antibodies that bind to virus particles.

Describe both processes and assess the effectiveness of each model in representing the process.
questions.answer:
**Model 1: phagocytosis.** A macrophage (a white blood cell) engulfs an invading bacterium and destroys it. This is part of the innate (non-specific) immune response. The macrophage then displays the antigen on MHC markers on its membrane and releases interleukin-1 to activate specific helper T cells (the adaptive response), which activates both the humoral and cell-mediated responses specific to the antigen.

*Assessment:* the model effectively shows the macrophage engulfing the bacteria. But it does not show what attracts phagocytes to the bacteria, nor what happens next (how the antigen is displayed and how that activates other parts of the immune system). Overall, it is only partly effective.

**Model 2: the humoral (antibody-mediated) response.** Plasma B cells release antibodies that are specific to the invading virus. The antibodies bind to the antigens on the virus to form an antigen–antibody complex, which destroys the virus, through neutralisation of binding sites, agglutination (which makes phagocytosis easier) or activation of the complement system, causing cell lysis.

*Assessment:* the model effectively shows plasma B cells producing antibodies and how the antibodies attach to the virus. It does not show how plasma B cells are activated, how the antibodies work, that antibodies are specific, or the production of memory B cells. Overall, it is only partly effective.

Overall, both models illustrate aspects of the immune response but neither shows how each process is activated or how they work together to destroy pathogens, so neither fully represents the whole process.

questions.question: A certain cell is known to be eukaryotic, heterotrophic and capable of causing disease. Which of the following is it likely to be?
questions.answer: Fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs and some cause disease. A macrophage is eukaryotic and heterotrophic but is not a pathogen; bacteria are prokaryotic; viruses are not cells.
options: a macrophage
a bacterium
a fungus
a virus

questions.question: One difference between T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes is:
questions.answer: B-lymphocytes (plasma cells) secrete antibodies (humoral response), while T-lymphocytes (cytotoxic T cells) destroy infected body cells (cell-mediated response). Both form memory cells, and neither produces antigens.
options: Only B-lymphocytes can produce memory cells.
B-lymphocytes produce antibodies and T-lymphocytes attack infected cells.
Only B-lymphocytes can produce antigens.
B-lymphocytes attack pathogens and T-lymphocytes attack tumour cells.

questions.question: The woolly mammoth was a large mammal that became extinct approximately 4000 years ago. Reduced genetic diversity associated with a small population size contributed to the extinction of this species and was probably due to:
questions.answer: Genetic drift (random changes in allele frequencies) has its strongest effect in small populations and reduces genetic diversity. Gene flow would increase diversity.
options: artificial selection.
gene flow.
mutation.
genetic drift.

questions.question: The approximate number of amino acids that could be coded for by a fully processed mRNA molecule comprising 1500 nucleotides is:
questions.answer: Each amino acid is coded by a codon of 3 nucleotides: $1500 \div 3 = 500$ amino acids.

questions.question: Errors in the production of insulin by the pancreas can cause serious metabolic disorders in the body. Which of the following is NOT a consequence of increased insulin concentration in the blood?
questions.answer: Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting glycogen formation in the liver, glucose uptake by muscle and fat cells and conversion of glucose to fat. Glucagon is made in the pancreas, not the liver, and its release is stimulated by low blood glucose, so it is not increased by high insulin.
options: increased synthesis of glucagon in the liver
increased production of glycogen by the liver
increased uptake of glucose by muscle and fat cells
increased conversion of glucose to fat in fat cells

questions.question:
The following flowchart is used to identify unknown pathogens. Some of the labels are missing. Which of the following rows correctly identifies the missing labels?

| | W | X | Y | Z |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | Proteins | Viruses | Prokaryotes | Eukaryotes |
| (B) | Prions | Viruses | Bacteria | Fungi |
| (C) | Prions | Viruses | Fungi | Bacteria |
| (D) | Viruses | Proteins | Prokaryotes | Fungi |
questions.answer: Non-cellular pathogens that do not contain nucleic acid are prions (W); those that do are viruses (X). Among cellular pathogens, microscopic ones without membrane-bound organelles are bacteria (Y), and microscopic eukaryotes with a rigid chitin cell wall are fungi (Z); protozoans are the eukaryotes without a cell wall.
options: Row A
Row B
Row C
Row D

questions.question:
Myrtle rust (*Austropuccinia psidii*) is a fungal disease that attacks the soft, actively growing leaves, shoot tips and young stems of *Eucalyptus* and other Myrtaceae plants. The disease produces small purple spots which later develop masses of bright yellow spores.

Eucalypts have a number of mechanisms that help them resist or respond to infection by myrtle rust. They have thick bark and cell walls reinforced with pectin and lignin. Their leaves produce eucalyptus oil, which has antifungal properties. When receptors on the eucalypt's cell walls detect fungal markers, those cells produce more structural protein to reinforce their cell walls. Cells inside the plant showing fungal antigens are flooded with oxygen, increasing their rate of respiration and causing them to 'burn up'.

Which of the following is a general induced response of *Eucalyptus* to the myrtle rust?
questions.answer: An induced response happens only after infection is detected. Producing extra structural protein to reinforce the cell walls is triggered by detecting fungal markers. Thick bark, thick cell walls and eucalyptus oil are always present (passive, pre-existing defences), and the young tissue is where the fungus attacks.
options: the thick bark and thick cell walls
the production of eucalyptus oil
the production of structural protein
the actively growing leaves, shoot tips and young stems

questions.question:
Beta-globin is a component of the haemoglobin protein found in red blood cells. The non-coding (template) strand in the gene for beta-globin begins with the following DNA sequence:

CACGTGGACTGAGGACTC

Sickle cell anaemia is a genetic condition caused by the substitution mutation of the 17th nucleotide in this sequence (T) and the resulting change this has on the amino acid sequence. The amino acid glutamic acid (GLU) produced in 'normal' fully functional beta-globin is changed to a valine (VAL) in sickle cell anaemia.

What kind of mutation has occurred to cause sickle cell anaemia?
questions.answer: A single nucleotide was substituted for another, which is a point mutation (a substitution). A frameshift needs an insertion or deletion, and a chromosomal mutation involves whole chromosomes or large segments.
options: a chromosomal mutation
a point mutation
a frameshift mutation
a somatic mutation

questions.question:
Beta-globin is a component of the haemoglobin protein found in red blood cells. The non-coding (template) strand in the gene for beta-globin begins with the following DNA sequence:

CACGTGGACTGAGGACTC

Sickle cell anaemia is a genetic condition caused by the substitution mutation of the 17th nucleotide in this sequence (T) and the resulting change this has on the amino acid sequence. The amino acid glutamic acid (GLU) produced in 'normal' fully functional beta-globin is changed to a valine (VAL) in sickle cell anaemia.

Using the codon table provided, what nucleotide base was substituted for thymine to produce the sickle cell anaemia mutation?
questions.answer: The template strand is CAC GTG GAC TGA GGA CTC, giving mRNA codons GUG CAC CUG ACU CCU GAG (the 6th codon is GAG = Glu). The 17th nucleotide is the T in the last template triplet CTC. The mutant codon must be Val (GUG, GUC, GUA or GUU), so the mRNA changes GAG $\to$ GUG: the middle base A becomes U, so on the template strand T becomes **A** (CTC $\to$ CAC).
options: Adenine
Thymine
Guanine
Cytosine

questions.question:
The following diagram shows homologous chromosomes as two pairs of sister chromatids labelled with alleles A and a, B and b, and C and c.

Which of the following statements is consistent with the process shown?
