the ability of microbes to generate spontaneously.
the most effective antibiotic treatment for a particular disease.
questions.answer: Koch's postulates are the criteria used to establish that a particular microbe causes a particular infectious disease.

questions.question: What is the role of the helper T-cell?
options: Secrete proteins known as antibodies, which act to neutralise the extracellular pathogen
Once activated, will release cytokines to activate the humoral and cell-mediated immune response
Clone themselves and remain in the body to respond to future exposure from the same pathogen.
Produce many copies of themselves, travel to the site of infection and release cytokines to destroy the infected cell.
questions.answer: Helper T cells, once activated by an antigen-presenting cell, release cytokines that activate B cells (humoral response) and cytotoxic T cells (cell-mediated response). A describes plasma cells, C memory cells and D cytotoxic T cells.

questions.question:
*Helicobacter pylori* is a bacterial pathogen known to cause stomach infections and ulcers. It uses chemotaxis (movement along a concentration gradient) to move through the stomach's acidic mucus and bind to the less acidic epithelial cells underneath, helped by its flagella which allow it to move in a screw-like motion through the mucus lining. It also secretes *urease*, an enzyme that helps to neutralise the acid around it.

Flagella and urease production in *Helicobacter pylori* represent which of the following?
options: Adaptations to create an acidic environment
Adaptations to survive and move through its environment
Physical and chemical changes that occur in host cells
The host response to infection
questions.answer: Flagella let the bacterium move through the mucus and urease neutralises the acid around it: both are pathogen adaptations for surviving and moving in the host.

questions.question:
The following photograph shows the results of an experiment designed to compare the efficacy of different antibiotics against a particular strain of bacteria which had been evenly inoculated across the agar plate. The antibiotics present in each disc are labelled A to E.

What conclusion can be drawn from the photograph?
options: Antibiotic D is the most effective against that strain of bacteria.
Antibiotic B is the most effective against that strain of bacteria.
Antibiotic B is the most effective antibiotic.
Antibiotic D is a wide spectrum antibiotic.
questions.answer: Disc D has the largest clear zone of inhibition, so it is the most effective against this strain. Only one strain was tested, so nothing can be said about other bacteria (C, D).

questions.question: The diagram below represents one aspect of the adaptive immune system response in humans. Which of the following correctly identifies A and B?
options: A: Phagocytes; B: Antigens
A: Plasma cells; B: Antibodies
A: Macrophages; B: Virus particles
A: Antigens; B: Antibodies
questions.answer: A shows particles bearing surface antigens; B shows Y-shaped antibodies; C shows the antibodies binding the antigens (forming clumps).

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a negative feedback mechanism?
options: A system of homeostatic regulation in which an increase in one factor triggers a pathway that counteracts the increase
A system of homeostatic regulation in which factors oscillate around a set point
A system of homeostatic regulation in which the nervous system counteracts changes
A system of homeostatic regulation in which an increase in one factor triggers a pathway that leads to further increase in that factor
questions.answer: In negative feedback the response opposes (counteracts) the change, returning the variable towards its set point. D describes positive feedback.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly identifies the components of a thermoregulatory negative feedback loop (stimulus; control centre; response)?
options: Increased temperature; hypothalamus; vasodilation
Decreased temperature; hypothalamus; vasodilation
Decreased temperature; hippocampus; vasoconstriction
Increased temperature; pancreas; vasoconstriction
questions.answer: The hypothalamus is the thermoregulatory control centre; a rise in body temperature causes vasodilation of skin arterioles so more heat is lost.

questions.question:
Use the pedigree below.

Identify the mode of inheritance.
questions.answer: **Autosomal recessive.** Unaffected parents (II-1 × II-2 and II-5 × II-6) have affected children, so the trait is recessive; an affected daughter (III-3) has an unaffected father, so it is not X-linked.

questions.question:
Use the pedigree below. The trait is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

Individual II-3 wants to conceive a child with an affected female. Show your working to calculate the phenotypic AND genotypic ratio of their potential offspring.
questions.answer:
Key: $H$ = unaffected (dominant) allele, $h$ = affected (recessive) allele.

II-3 is unaffected but his mother (I-1) is affected ($hh$), so he must have received an $h$ from her: II-3 is **heterozygous, $Hh$**. The affected female is homozygous recessive, $hh$.

| | $H$ | $h$ |
|---|---|---|
| $h$ | $Hh$ | $hh$ |
| $h$ | $Hh$ | $hh$ |

**Genotypic ratio:** 1 $Hh$ (heterozygous) : 1 $hh$ (homozygous recessive), i.e. 50% : 50%.

**Phenotypic ratio:** 1 unaffected (carrier) : 1 affected, i.e. 50% : 50%.

questions.question:
The diagram below shows the basal body temperature and hormone levels during a 28-day menstrual cycle.

Identify the day on which ovulation would most likely occur.
questions.answer: **Day 14** — immediately after the LH surge (peak of LH and FSH) and as basal body temperature rises. (Day 13 was also accepted.)

questions.question:
The diagram below shows the basal body temperature and hormone levels during a 28-day menstrual cycle.

Outline the role of progesterone once an egg has been fertilised.
questions.answer: After ovulation the corpus luteum secretes progesterone. Once the egg is fertilised, progesterone maintains and further thickens the endometrium (lining of the uterus) so that the embryo can implant, and after implantation it continues to maintain the endometrium and inhibits uterine contractions and further FSH/LH release, so no new follicles develop and the pregnancy is maintained.

questions.question:
The diagram below shows the basal body temperature and hormone levels during a 28-day menstrual cycle.

Hypopituitarism is a disorder in which the pituitary gland is unable to produce hormones such as FSH and LH. Use the diagram and your understanding of female reproductive hormones to explain the impact this disorder would have on a woman's menstrual cycle and ability to conceive a child.
questions.answer:
FSH and LH are released by the anterior pituitary. FSH stimulates the development of follicles in the ovary (each containing an egg), and the developing follicle secretes oestrogen, which rises through the follicular phase on the graph. The sharp LH (and FSH) surge around day 14 triggers ovulation and the formation of the corpus luteum, which then secretes progesterone in the luteal phase.

With hypopituitarism, FSH and LH are not produced, so follicles do not mature, oestrogen stays low, there is no LH surge and therefore no ovulation, and no corpus luteum forms to produce progesterone. The endometrium is not built up, so the menstrual cycle becomes irregular or stops (no menstruation). Because no egg is released and the uterus is not prepared for implantation, the woman's fertility is reduced — she would be unable to conceive naturally.

questions.question:
A family had a child with cystic fibrosis, a heritable, autosomal recessive genetic disorder that results in the production of highly sticky mucus in both the lungs and digestive tract and can prove life-threatening. The father of the child is known to have a family history of cystic fibrosis, however, he does not have the condition. It was not known whether the mother had a family history of cystic fibrosis, but she does not have the condition.

The family requested a genetic test and the following DNA profile was obtained.

Identify which segment from the DNA profile contains the allele that is responsible for cystic fibrosis and provide a reason for your selection.
questions.answer:
**Segment 4.** Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive, so the affected child must have inherited a copy of the CF allele from *each* parent, and both unaffected parents must be carriers. The segment containing the allele must therefore be present in the mother, the father and the child. Segment 4 is the only band shared by all three (segment 1 is in both parents but not the child; segments 2 and 5 come only from the mother and segment 7 only from the father). This also shows the mother must be a carrier.

*(Markers also accepted segment 1 if argued as the normal allele that the child is missing.)*

questions.question: Outline the process of DNA profiling.
questions.answer:
DNA profiling compares non-coding regions of DNA called short tandem repeats (STRs), where the number of repeats varies between individuals.

1. DNA is extracted from a sample (e.g. blood or cheek cells).
2. The STR regions are amplified by the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using primers that flank them, producing many copies (restriction enzymes can be used to cut DNA into fragments).
3. The fragments are separated by size using gel electrophoresis — DNA is negatively charged and moves towards the positive electrode, with shorter fragments travelling further.
4. The fragments are made visible (stained or labelled) to give a banding pattern, which is compared between individuals: related individuals share more bands, and each child's bands must all come from one or other parent.

questions.question:
In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick described the molecular structure of DNA. Six years earlier, in 1947, J. Michael Creeth published a paper in which he provided evidence for the presence of hydrogen bonding between purine and pyrimidine bases in DNA. This knowledge, now referred to as complementary base pairing, paved the way for the determination of the structure of the DNA double helix and is crucial to understanding nucleic acid function and current biotechnological processes based on DNA.

Describe the role of complementary base pairing in the process of polypeptide synthesis and discuss the importance of complementary base pairing in ONE of the following biotechnological processes: PCR (polymerase chain reaction) OR CRISPR-Cas9 editing.
questions.answer:
**Complementary base pairing** is the specific hydrogen bonding between a purine and a pyrimidine: in DNA adenine pairs with thymine (A–T) and guanine with cytosine (G–C); in RNA uracil replaces thymine (A–U). Because each base can pair with only one partner, one strand acts as an exact template for another, so the genetic code can be copied accurately.

**Polypeptide synthesis.** In *transcription*, the DNA unwinds and RNA polymerase adds free RNA nucleotides that are complementary to the template strand (A–U, T–A, G–C, C–G), producing an mRNA copy of the gene's code. The mRNA leaves the nucleus and binds to a ribosome. In *translation*, each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that is complementary to an mRNA codon; the anticodon pairs with the codon so that the correct amino acid is brought into position and joined by peptide bonds. Complementary base pairing therefore ensures the DNA code is transcribed and translated exactly into the correct amino acid sequence; an error would change the polypeptide.

**PCR.** PCR makes millions of exact copies of a DNA sequence from a small sample (e.g. for DNA profiling). The DNA is heated (~95 °C) to break the hydrogen bonds between the strands (denaturation). On cooling (~55 °C), short primers bind (anneal) to their *complementary* sequences at each end of the target region. Taq DNA polymerase (~72 °C) then extends from the primers, adding free nucleotides complementary to each template strand. Complementary pairing is essential: it makes the primers bind only at the target sequence, and it ensures each new strand is an exact copy. Repeating the cycle doubles the target each time.

*(Alternative — CRISPR-Cas9: a guide RNA whose sequence is complementary to the target DNA leads the Cas9 enzyme to that exact location, where it cuts the DNA; complementary base pairing therefore gives the editing its precision, allowing a gene to be disabled or replaced, e.g. potentially correcting the cystic fibrosis allele.)*

questions.question: Discuss how the processes of gamete formation and fertilisation contribute to variation in the offspring in humans.
questions.answer:
Gametes are formed by **meiosis** in the testes and ovaries: one diploid cell undergoes two divisions to form haploid gametes with half the chromosome number. Meiosis produces genetically different gametes in two main ways:

- **Crossing over:** during prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair up and non-sister chromatids exchange segments at chiasmata, so each chromosome ends up with a new combination of maternal and paternal alleles.
- **Independent assortment / random segregation:** in metaphase I each homologous pair lines up independently of the others, so chromosomes (and the alleles on them) are randomly separated into the gametes — in humans $2^{23}$ (over 8 million) combinations are possible without crossing over.

**Fertilisation** then joins one sperm and one egg at random, combining two genetically unique gametes from two different parents. This multiplies the possible combinations further, so every offspring (except identical twins) has a unique genotype. Together, meiosis and random fertilisation are the major sources of variation in offspring.

questions.question: Phenotypic expression of certain genotypes can also be affected by environmental factors. Discuss an example of a trait in a named organism that is affected by both genes and environment.
questions.answer:
In **Himalayan rabbits** (*Oryctolagus cuniculus*), fur colour is controlled by a gene for a temperature-sensitive enzyme that produces dark pigment. The enzyme only works at temperatures below core body temperature, so dark pigment is produced only in the cooler extremities (ears, nose, feet, tail) while the rest of the body is white. If a patch of fur on the back is shaved and kept cold, it regrows dark. The rabbit's genes determine whether it can make the pigment, but the environment (temperature) determines where the gene is expressed.

*(Other accepted examples: Siamese cat fur colour; hydrangea flower colour depending on soil pH; honeybee larvae becoming queens when fed royal jelly; human height depending on genes and nutrition.)*

questions.question:
The cheetah (*Acinonyx jubatus*) is a vulnerable species of large cat, known for being the fastest land animal. Since the 19th century, it is estimated that the cheetah population has declined from 100,000 to approximately 8,000 cheetahs.

The cheetah faces extinction due to climate change, hunting by humans and habitat destruction. They also have a low rate of reproductive success. Present-day cheetahs also have low genetic variability, increasing the rate of inbreeding among individuals.

The distribution of subspecies of the cheetah, as of 2015, is shown below.

The following could have a potential effect on the future gene pool of the cheetah: mutation, gene flow, genetic drift.

Explain how each of the above could impact the gene pool of the cheetah.
questions.answer:
The **gene pool** is the total set of alleles in a population; its allele frequencies can be changed by mutation, gene flow and genetic drift.

**Mutation** is a permanent change to the DNA sequence, occurring randomly or caused by mutagens such as UV radiation or chemicals. Only germ-line mutations (in cells that form gametes) are passed to offspring and can enter the gene pool. Mutation is the only source of new alleles, so over time it could add variation to the cheetah's very small gene pool. However, mutation rates are very low, so this would happen slowly; most new mutations are neutral or harmful, and in a small, inbred population harmful recessive alleles are more likely to be expressed in homozygous offspring, which may further reduce reproductive success. A beneficial mutation (e.g. one improving heat tolerance as the climate changes) could increase in frequency through natural selection.

**Gene flow** is the movement of alleles between populations when individuals migrate and interbreed. The map shows four subspecies in isolated ranges. Where ranges are close (e.g. some *A. j. soemmeringii* and *A. j. jubatus* populations in East Africa), gene flow could introduce new alleles, increasing genetic variation and reducing inbreeding. However, *A. j. hecki* (north-west Africa) and *A. j. venaticus* (Iran) are geographically isolated, and habitat destruction fragments ranges further, so gene flow is reduced. These populations will keep losing variation and diverging from one another; conservation programs could restore gene flow by translocating individuals or using artificial insemination.

**Genetic drift** is a random change in allele frequencies from one generation to the next due to chance, and it has the greatest effect in small populations. The decline from about 100 000 to 8000 cheetahs is a **bottleneck**: the survivors carried only a fraction of the original alleles, which explains the low genetic variability. Because the population — and especially the isolated subspecies — is now small, chance events (hunting, disease, climate-driven droughts) will cause alleles to be lost or fixed randomly, further reducing variation regardless of whether alleles are beneficial. Small isolated groups (as with *A. j. hecki* and *A. j. venaticus*) may also experience the founder effect. Overall, drift will reduce the gene pool's diversity and increase inbreeding, lowering the cheetah's ability to adapt to environmental change.

questions.question: Endangered species are under threat from many factors, including human-induced climate change, habitat destruction and hunting. Outline an example of how population genetics data or genetic technologies are being used to assist in the conservation of a named endangered animal or plant species.
questions.answer:
The **northern quoll** (*Dasyurus hallucatus*) is an endangered Australian marsupial. Scientists use genome sequencing and DNA markers to measure the genetic variation within and between wild quoll populations. These population genetics data identify populations that have lost diversity through isolation and inbreeding, and are used to select genetically diverse, unrelated individuals for captive breeding and for translocation to new or existing populations. This maintains genetic diversity, reduces inbreeding and helps the species adapt to threats such as cane toads.

*(Other accepted examples: DNA profiling of ivory to trace the origin of poached African elephants; genome studies of koala populations, including immune genes to develop a chlamydia vaccine.)*

questions.question:
The following diagram illustrates the general features of a technique used in biotechnology.

The diagram shows some of the forms in which DNA occurs in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Describe two differences between eukaryotic and prokaryotic forms of DNA.
questions.answer:
Any two of:

- **Location:** prokaryotic DNA is found free in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid, whereas eukaryotic DNA is enclosed within a membrane-bound nucleus (with small amounts in mitochondria and chloroplasts).
- **Shape:** prokaryotes have a single circular chromosome, whereas eukaryotes have multiple linear chromosomes.
- **Plasmids:** prokaryotes often contain small, extra-chromosomal circular DNA molecules called plasmids; these are generally absent in eukaryotes.
- **Packaging:** eukaryotic DNA is wound around histone proteins to form chromatin, whereas prokaryotic DNA is not associated with histones (it is 'naked').
- **Non-coding DNA:** eukaryotic genomes contain large amounts of non-coding and repetitive DNA, including introns, whereas prokaryotic genomes are compact with few non-coding regions and no introns.

(Both are double-stranded DNA.)

questions.question:
The following diagram illustrates the general features of a technique used in biotechnology. A gene of interest is inserted into a bacterial plasmid (cut with a restriction enzyme) to form a recombinant plasmid, which is taken up by a host cell (a plant cell or a bacterium) so that the host's genome carries the new gene.

Using examples, justify the application of the process illustrated above in agriculture and medicine.
questions.answer:
The diagram shows **recombinant DNA technology**: a gene of interest is cut out with a restriction enzyme, inserted into a plasmid cut with the same enzyme and joined with DNA ligase, and the recombinant plasmid is used as a vector to carry the gene into a host cell. The host becomes a **transgenic organism** that expresses a gene from another species. This is justified because a specific, desirable trait can be added far more quickly and precisely than by selective breeding, and across species boundaries.

**Agriculture**

- **Bt cotton:** the gene for the Bt toxin from the bacterium *Bacillus thuringiensis* is transferred into cotton using a recombinant plasmid in *Agrobacterium tumefaciens*. The cotton plants produce a protein that kills leaf-eating caterpillars (e.g. *Helicoverpa*), so far less insecticide is sprayed, reducing costs and environmental damage while increasing yield.
- **Herbicide-resistant crops** (e.g. Roundup Ready soybean and canola) carry a bacterial gene for a herbicide-tolerant enzyme, so weeds can be controlled without damaging the crop. Other examples include Golden Rice, engineered with genes for β-carotene to reduce vitamin A deficiency.

These applications are justified because they increase productivity and food security while reducing chemical use, although concerns such as reduced biodiversity and pest resistance must be managed.

**Medicine**

- **Human insulin:** the human insulin gene is inserted into plasmids and taken up by *E. coli* (or yeast). The transgenic bacteria multiply rapidly and secrete human insulin, which is purified for people with type 1 diabetes. It is identical to human insulin, so it causes fewer allergic reactions than insulin extracted from cattle or pigs, and it can be produced cheaply, reliably and in large quantities.
- **Vaccines and other proteins:** genes for a pathogen antigen (e.g. hepatitis B surface antigen) are inserted into yeast to produce safe subunit vaccines; transgenic sheep produce human blood-clotting factors in their milk.

These applications are justified because they provide safe, plentiful and affordable treatments that save lives. Overall, the ability to transfer a single beneficial gene precisely into a host makes recombinant DNA technology highly valuable in both agriculture and medicine.

questions.question:
A plant pathologist observed brown spots developing on the leaves of a lemon tree and wanted to determine the cause of the disease. The pathologist suspected the tree was suffering from a bacterial disease, caused by infection with *Xanthomonas citri*.

Describe a method the pathologist could use to test the hypothesis that the suspected bacterium is the cause of the disease.
questions.answer:
Use **Koch's postulates**:

1. Examine diseased leaves and confirm the suspected bacterium is present in all diseased tissue (and absent from healthy leaves), then **isolate** it from the lesions.
2. Grow the isolated bacterium in **pure culture** on a sterile nutrient agar plate.
3. **Inoculate** healthy, disease-free lemon leaves/plants with the bacterium from the pure culture (keeping uninoculated control plants under the same conditions). The inoculated plants should develop the same brown spots as the original diseased tree, while the controls stay healthy.
4. **Re-isolate** the bacterium from the newly diseased leaves, grow it in pure culture and compare it with the original culture; if it is identical, *X. citri* is confirmed as the cause.

questions.question: Explain the response of a named Australian plant to a named pathogen.
questions.answer: The oomycete *Phytophthora cinnamomi* infects the roots of jarrah (*Eucalyptus marginata*), causing jarrah dieback. When the pathogen's hyphae invade the root tissue, the plant recognises it and responds by depositing extra **lignin** (and callose) in the cell walls of cells around the infection. The thickened, lignified walls act as a physical barrier that hyphae cannot easily penetrate, which limits the spread of the pathogen from cell to cell within the root and so slows the damage to the water-conducting tissue. Resistant jarrah plants lignify their cell walls more rapidly than susceptible ones, which is why they survive infection.

questions.question:
Human African trypanosomiasis (HAT), commonly known as sleeping sickness, is a disease caused by the protozoan *Trypanosoma brucei*, and is carried by the tsetse fly, *Glossina* sp. There are two trypanosome subspecies that affect humans: *T. brucei gambiense* and *T. brucei rhodesiense*. A third subspecies, *T. brucei brucei*, only affects cattle. All humans possess a protein (APO L1) that protects them against infection with *T. brucei brucei* by causing the trypanosomes to break open before they can cause disease.

The life cycle of the two subspecies that affect humans is illustrated below.

The figure illustrates proliferation by binary fission at various stages in the life cycle of the trypanosome. Until recently, there was little evidence of sexual reproduction in the life cycle of trypanosomes.

Discuss the benefits to the trypanosome of carrying out asexual reproduction in the human host.
questions.answer: Asexual reproduction by binary fission is fast and needs only one parent, so trypanosomes can multiply rapidly in the blood, lymph and spinal fluid. This rapidly builds up large numbers of parasites in the bloodstream, increasing the chance that a tsetse fly will take them up in a blood meal and transmit them to a new host. In addition, the human body is a relatively stable environment, and the offspring are genetically identical clones, so the combination of characteristics that allows the parent to survive in the human bloodstream is passed on unchanged to all offspring.

questions.question:
*Trypanosoma brucei* is a protozoan parasite that causes human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness); it multiplies by binary fission in humans and is transmitted by the tsetse fly. In recent studies, scientists have identified proteins associated with meiosis in trypanosomes and it is believed that the sexual phase occurs in the salivary glands of the tsetse fly. The discovery of hybrid trypanosomes in humans and haploid trypanosomes in tsetse flies provided further evidence of sexual reproduction in trypanosomes.

While these discoveries supported the idea that trypanosomes have a sexual phase, they have caused concern among epidemiologists over the potential for trypanosomes to develop drug resistance. Why would these recent discoveries cause this concern among epidemiologists?
questions.answer: Sexual reproduction (meiosis and the fusion of gametes to form hybrids) produces offspring with new combinations of alleles, increasing genetic variation in the trypanosome population. If any variant carries alleles that confer drug resistance, these can be combined and spread to many offspring during the sexual phase in the tsetse fly and then passed to many human hosts. When drugs are used, they act as a selective pressure: resistant trypanosomes survive and reproduce, so the frequency of resistance increases and drug-resistant strains could eventually dominate.

questions.question:
Human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) is caused by the protozoan *Trypanosoma brucei* and is transmitted to humans when an infected tsetse fly (*Glossina* sp.) takes a blood meal. Cattle and possibly wild ungulates act as reservoirs.

Describe TWO strategies, other than administration of drugs or vaccines, that could be implemented to help control the spread of human African trypanosomiasis.
questions.answer:
1. **Reduce the vector population:** spray insecticide in tsetse fly breeding and resting areas, or use insecticide-treated traps and targets, so fewer flies are available to transmit the parasite. Releasing sterile male flies (sterile insect technique) also reduces reproduction of the flies.
2. **Prevent bites:** people in affected areas can wear long, neutral-coloured clothing and use insect repellent and bed nets/screens, so infected flies cannot feed on them. (Treating cattle reservoirs with insecticide also reduces transmission.)

questions.question:
Human African trypanosomiasis (HAT) is caused by the protozoan *Trypanosoma brucei*. In an analysis of current strategies for the eradication of HAT, Babokhov and co-workers wrote:

> "The biggest obstacle in the fight against HAT is that there is still no effective vaccine against both human pathogenic subspecies. Creating any sort of vaccine against trypanosomes is difficult due to antigenic variation. The constant changes of the VSG [variant surface glycoprotein] coat allow the parasite to evade immune defences."

Justify this statement, using your knowledge of vaccine function.
questions.answer:
A vaccine introduces an antigen of the pathogen (e.g. as an attenuated or killed pathogen, a purified protein subunit or mRNA) without causing disease. This triggers a primary adaptive immune response: helper T cells activate B cells specific to that antigen, which form plasma cells that produce antibodies and long-lived memory B and T cells. On later exposure, the memory cells recognise the same antigen and mount a rapid, strong secondary response.

This protection relies on antigen–antibody **specificity** — antibodies and memory cells only recognise the exact antigen used in the vaccine. Trypanosomes constantly change their VSG surface coat, so the antigens they display keep changing. Antibodies and memory cells produced in response to a vaccine containing one VSG would not bind to the new VSG variant, so the parasite evades the immune response. Therefore a single vaccine cannot give lasting protection, which justifies the statement.

questions.question:
Alpha-gal is a sugar molecule found in most mammals and mammalian products such as beef, pork, lamb, cow's milk products and gelatine. It is not found in primate mammals, including humans.

Alpha-gal syndrome (AGS) is a condition where an affected person will have a serious, life-threatening allergic reaction to food products containing alpha-gal sugar. The syndrome is triggered when a tick (a macroparasite) bites a mammal that produces the alpha-gal sugar and then bites a human.

Evidence suggests that after a human is bitten by such a tick, an immune response is triggered. This is because antibodies specific to the alpha-gal sugar are found in the blood of the affected person.

Describe the processes involved in the production of antibodies to the alpha-gal sugar.
questions.answer: On primary exposure, the tick bite introduces alpha-gal, which the body recognises as a foreign (non-self) **antigen**. **Antigen-presenting cells** (e.g. macrophages or dendritic cells) engulf the alpha-gal-containing material, process it and present the antigen on their surface (on MHC II markers). They travel to a lymph node, where the antigen is presented to a **helper T cell** with a matching receptor. The activated helper T cell releases **cytokines**, which activate a naïve **B cell** that has receptors specific to alpha-gal (and has bound the antigen). The activated B cell undergoes clonal selection and proliferation, dividing many times and differentiating into **plasma B cells** and memory B cells. The **plasma cells** secrete large quantities of antibodies specific to alpha-gal into the blood, while the **memory B cells** remain in the body. On later exposure (e.g. eating red meat), the memory cells rapidly produce more antibodies, triggering the allergic reaction.

questions.question:
Alpha-gal is a sugar molecule found in most mammals and mammalian products such as beef, pork, lamb, cow's milk products and gelatine. It is not found in primate mammals, including humans.

Alpha-gal syndrome (AGS) is a condition where an affected person will have a serious, life-threatening allergic reaction to food products containing alpha-gal sugar. The syndrome is triggered when a tick (a macroparasite) bites a mammal that produces the alpha-gal sugar and then bites a human.

Scientists have found that alpha-gal is unable to be passed from human to human. Is alpha-gal syndrome an infectious or non-infectious disease? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
**Alpha-gal syndrome is a non-infectious disease.** An infectious disease is caused by a pathogen (a disease-causing organism or agent such as a bacterium, virus or parasite) that invades a host, multiplies and can be transmitted from one host to another. A non-infectious disease is not caused by a pathogen and cannot be transmitted between people.

AGS is caused by the immune system's allergic response to a sugar molecule (alpha-gal), which is not a living, replicating pathogen. The tick only acts as a vector that transfers a molecule naturally found in non-primate mammal tissue into a human — the tick does not cause the disease by infecting the person. Since the condition cannot be passed from human to human, it is best classified as non-infectious (an allergy, i.e. an immune disorder caused by environmental exposure).

questions.question:
Type 1 diabetes is a condition in which the pancreas produces little or no insulin. The diagram below shows the negative feedback loop of glucose control in a person without Type 1 Diabetes.

With reference to the feedback loop, explain why a person with Type 1 Diabetes must inject insulin when they eat.
questions.answer:
Normal blood glucose level is about 90 mg/100 mL. After eating, glucose is absorbed and the blood glucose level increases (the stimulus). In a healthy person the beta cells of the pancreas detect this and release insulin into the blood. Insulin causes the liver to take up glucose and store it as glycogen and body cells to take up glucose, so the blood glucose level decreases back to the normal level — a negative feedback response.

In Type 1 diabetes the beta cells produce little or no insulin, so the top half of the loop cannot operate: after a meal, glucose is not taken up and stored, and blood glucose stays dangerously high (hyperglycaemia). By injecting insulin when they eat, the person replaces the missing hormone, allowing the liver and body cells to take up glucose so the blood glucose level returns to about 90 mg/100 mL and is maintained within tolerance limits.

questions.question:
The graph below shows the levels of glucose in the blood of a healthy individual over time. The two arrows indicate events that would influence the levels of blood glucose: one shows when the individual ate and the other when they exercised.

Identify which arrow indicates when the individual ate and which indicates when they exercised.
questions.answer: The **first arrow** (just before the large rise in blood glucose) is when the individual **ate**. The **second arrow** (just before blood glucose falls below its normal level) is when the individual **exercised**, as working muscles take up and use glucose.

questions.question:
The graph below shows the levels of glucose in the blood of a healthy individual over time. The two arrows indicate events that would influence the levels of blood glucose: one shows when the individual ate and the other when they exercised. The first arrow marks a meal and the second marks exercise.

Sketch the graph and add one labelled line to show how levels of insulin would change over the same period, and another labelled line to show how levels of glucagon would change over the same period. (The vertical scale is arbitrary.)
questions.answer:
- **Insulin** rises sharply soon after the meal, peaking at about the same time as (or just after) the glucose peak, then falls back to a low baseline as glucose returns to normal; it stays low during and after exercise.
- **Glucagon** falls after the meal while glucose is high, then rises after exercise when blood glucose drops below normal, peaking while glucose is at its lowest; it returns towards baseline as glucose recovers.

The two hormones change in opposite directions, each acting to return blood glucose to its set point.

prev.question:

questions.question:
A plant pathologist observed brown spots developing on the leaves of a lemon tree and wanted to determine the cause of the disease. The pathologist suspected the tree was suffering from a bacterial disease, caused by infection with *Xanthomonas citri*.

Outline TWO plant adaptations for defence against pathogens.
questions.answer:
1. Plants deposit **cell wall material** (e.g. callose or lignin) around pathogens to seal them off from the surrounding tissue.
2. Plants such as eucalypts store **oils** in their leaves, which act as chemical defences against fungal and bacterial pathogens.

questions.question:
A plant pathologist observed brown spots developing on the leaves of a lemon tree. The pathologist suspected the tree was suffering from a bacterial disease, caused by infection with *Xanthomonas citri*.

Describe the steps a pathologist could use to test the hypothesis that the suspected bacterium is the cause of the disease.
questions.answer:
Using Koch's postulates:
1. **Isolate** the suspected pathogen from the diseased area of the leaf.
2. **Grow** the suspected pathogen in pure culture.
3. **Infect** disease-free leaves with the cultured bacteria; the infected leaves should show the same symptoms as the original diseased leaves.
4. **Re-isolate** the bacteria from the newly infected leaves and grow them in culture; they should be identical to the pathogen in the first culture.

questions.question:
The cheetah (*Acinonyx jubatus*) is a vulnerable species of large cat, known for being the fastest land animal. Since the 19th century, it is estimated that the cheetah population has declined from 100,000 to approximately 8,000 cheetahs.

The cheetah faces extinction due to climate change, hunting by humans and habitat destruction. They also have a low rate of reproductive success.

The map shows the distribution of subspecies of the cheetah as of 2015.

Explain how gene flow and genetic drift could impact the future gene pool of the cheetah.
questions.answer:
**Gene flow** is the movement of alleles between populations when individuals migrate and breed. The map shows four subspecies. Where subspecies are widespread and close (*A.j. soemmeringii* and *A.j. jubatus*), gene flow can be high; this increases genetic variability, reduces inbreeding and increases the chance of survival. The isolated populations (*A.j. hecki* and *A.j. venaticus*) have limited gene flow, so they could diverge genetically, even to the point of speciation, which reduces population size and variability and increases inbreeding and harmful traits.

**Genetic drift** is a chance change in allele frequencies, with the strongest effect in small populations. The fall from 100,000 to about 8,000 cheetahs is a **bottleneck**: the survivors carry only a fraction of the original alleles, so genetic variability is low and will remain low even if numbers recover, with a higher risk of inbreeding and fewer beneficial alleles. If *A.j. hecki* and *A.j. venaticus* stay isolated, a **founder effect** could further reduce variation.

questions.question:
The cheetah (*Acinonyx jubatus*) is a vulnerable species of large cat, known for being the fastest land animal. Since the 19th century, it is estimated that the cheetah population has declined from 100,000 to approximately 8,000 cheetahs.

The cheetah faces extinction due to climate change, hunting by humans and habitat destruction. They also have a low rate of reproductive success.

The map shows the distribution of subspecies of the cheetah as of 2015.

Describe how DNA profiling can be used to show genetic diversity within a population.
questions.answer: DNA profiling looks at the number of short tandem repeats (STRs) at particular loci; individuals, and close relatives, have characteristic patterns. **Genetic diversity** is the extent to which individuals in a population carry different alleles. Profiling many individuals gives a measure of diversity: if the profiles are very similar, individuals are closely related and diversity is low; a wide range of profiles means high genetic diversity.

questions.question:
The cheetah (*Acinonyx jubatus*) is a vulnerable species of large cat, known for being the fastest land animal. Since the 19th century, it is estimated that the cheetah population has declined from 100,000 to approximately 8,000 cheetahs.

The cheetah faces extinction due to climate change, hunting by humans and habitat destruction. They also have a low rate of reproductive success.

The map shows the distribution of subspecies of the cheetah as of 2015.

Explain how information gained through DNA profiling of cheetah populations can help direct efforts to conserve them.
questions.answer: Genetic diversity is critical to survival: a diverse population is better able to survive climate change or disease because some individuals will have variants that resist it. Small, fragmented populations lose diversity through genetic drift. DNA profiling measures the diversity of each cheetah population, so conservation authorities can identify populations with low diversity and **move individuals between populations** (or manage breeding) to increase it.

questions.question: Compare the processes of DNA replication and Polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
questions.answer:
**Similarities:** both make copies of DNA; both use DNA polymerase to join free nucleotides to a template strand; both use complementary base pairing, and both are semi-conservative (each new molecule has one original and one new strand).

**Differences:** DNA replication occurs inside living cells and copies the whole genome, using helicase to unwind the DNA, while PCR occurs in vitro (in a machine) and copies only a target section of DNA, using heat to separate the strands. PCR needs primers and repeated heating/cooling cycles and doubles the DNA each cycle, whereas replication occurs once per cell cycle.

questions.question:
Influenza is an infectious respiratory disease. In humans, it can be caused by the influenza A or influenza B viruses.

Natural killer cells and cytotoxic T cells both play an important part in the human immune response to the virus causing influenza.

Compare the roles played by each of these two types of cells in the immune response to the influenza virus.
questions.answer:
**Natural killer (NK) cells** are part of the innate (second line) defence. They do not need antigen presentation, so they act early and rapidly, are non-specific, and kill infected cells in the early stages, limiting viral replication and spread to neighbouring cells.

**Cytotoxic T cells** are part of the adaptive (third line) defence. They act later, are specific: their receptors bind the antigen displayed on the infected cell.

**Similarities:** both recognise virally infected cells (displaying antigen on MHC-I) and kill them by releasing granules containing perforin and granzymes, which make pores in the target cell membrane and cause cell death (apoptosis).

questions.question:
The graph shows the distance between the sister chromatids of a replicated chromosome during a mitotic cell division.

Draw diagrams to show the arrangement of the chromosomes at 10 minutes, 15 minutes and at 20 minutes in a diploid cell containing four chromosomes. (Three empty circles are provided, labelled pattern at 10 min, 15 min and 20 min.)
questions.answer:
Draw a cell with **four chromosomes** in each circle.
- **10 min** (distance 0): chromosomes lined up on the equator with sister chromatids still joined (metaphase).
- **15 min** (distance about 20 $\mu$m): sister chromatids have separated and are moving to opposite poles (early anaphase).
- **20 min** (distance about 40 $\mu$m): the chromatids are at opposite poles, twice as far apart as at 15 min (late anaphase).

questions.question:
Artificial insulin has revolutionised the treatment of diabetes, providing an effective means of managing blood glucose levels.

Before restriction enzymes cut the insulin gene, mature mRNA coding for insulin must first be converted to DNA. The process by which this occurs is called reverse transcription.

With reference to differences between eukaryotic and prokaryotic DNA, explain why reverse transcription is necessary for the production of artificial insulin.
questions.answer:
Eukaryotic DNA (including the human insulin gene) contains protein-coding regions (**exons**) and non-coding regions (**introns**); introns are removed by splicing before the gene is expressed. Prokaryotic DNA has no introns and prokaryotes do not undergo splicing.

Artificial insulin is made by inserting the human gene into a bacterial plasmid. Bacteria lack the machinery to remove introns from pre-mRNA, so the human gene with its introns could not be processed correctly. Mature mRNA has already had its introns removed, so it is used as a template, and reverse transcriptase makes DNA (cDNA) without introns, which the bacteria can express to make functional insulin.

questions.question:
E-cigarettes operate by vaporising a nicotine-containing liquid into an aerosol, which is then inhaled by the user.

Since their first introduction to broad global markets in 2007, use has become increasingly common, particularly among youth. They were initially introduced as an alternative to traditional tobacco smoking, with the idea that it could potentially be less harmful due to the absence of tar and combustion products found in tobacco smoke. However, concerns have arisen about the safety and health risks associated with vaping.

Describe and justify an epidemiological study that could be carried out to investigate whether vaping using e-cigarettes causes lung disease.
questions.answer:
**Hypothesis:** vaping with e-cigarettes increases the risk of lung disease.

**Study: a cohort study** (like the British Doctors' Study).
- Recruit a **large sample** of people with no lung disease, and record their vaping status (e.g. vapers who have never smoked, and a **control group** of non-vapers who have never smoked). A large sample gives reliable results and allows trends to be seen.
- Follow the groups over many years, regularly recording lung disease (e.g. by surveys and lung function tests). Following people forward in time shows that vaping comes before the disease, which supports a causal link.
- **Control other variables** such as age, sex, smoking history and exposure to air pollution (match the groups or record and adjust for them), so differences are due to vaping.
- Use **statistical analysis** to compare the rates of lung disease in the groups (e.g. relative risk) and judge whether the difference is significant.

questions.question:
Foot-and-mouth disease, a contagious viral disease for cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, resurfaced in Indonesia in May 2022 after the country had been declared free of it for over 30 years. What makes FMD virus so remarkable is its environmental resistance. It can persist on many inanimate objects, such as equipment used with livestock, people's clothing and shoes, on the tyres of vehicles and in livestock transport. It can also persist in livestock feed and livestock products, such as meat and hides. There is no cure for FMD.

Outline the possible effects of FMD being spread to Australia.
questions.answer: Animal welfare: painful lesions on the feet and mouth cause lameness, reduced feeding and suffering. Agriculture: there is no cure, so infected and exposed animals would have to be destroyed, which is expensive and disruptive; meat and dairy production would fall. Economy: Australia is a major exporter of livestock and animal products, so trading partners would ban exports, causing major losses for farmers, processors, exporters and related industries, and it could take time to regain market access.

questions.question:
Foot-and-mouth disease, a contagious viral disease for cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, resurfaced in Indonesia in May 2022 after the country had been declared free of it for over 30 years. What makes FMD virus so remarkable is its environmental resistance. It can persist on many inanimate objects, such as equipment used with livestock, people's clothing and shoes, on the tyres of vehicles and in livestock transport. It can also persist in livestock feed and livestock products, such as meat and hides. There is no cure for FMD.

Outline a strategy that could prevent the spread of FMD to Australia.
questions.answer: **Strengthen quarantine and biosecurity at the border:** restrict the import of animal products (meat, dairy, hides) from Indonesia and other affected countries, and increase screening of high-risk goods (e.g. hides, meat, dairy, clothing, farming equipment) and travellers entering Australia, with stronger clearance requirements (e.g. declaring footwear that has been on farms and disinfecting it). Awareness campaigns and increased disease surveillance in northern Australia (WA, NT and northern Queensland) would also help detect it early.

questions.question: Describe TWO mechanisms in plants that allow water balance to be maintained.
questions.answer:
1. **Water uptake at the root hairs:** plants change the osmotic gradient by altering the concentration of dissolved solutes in the root hair cells; a higher solute concentration increases water uptake by osmosis.
2. **Water loss through the stomata:** plants alter the transpiration rate by changing the turgor of the guard cells. When water levels fall, the hormone **abscisic acid** is released and causes the stomata to close; when there is enough water the guard cells become turgid, bend and open the stomata.

(Adaptations such as sunken stomata or reduced leaf size also reduce water loss.)

questions.question: Use an example to outline the role of the nervous system in maintaining homeostasis.
questions.answer:
The nervous system detects changes and counteracts them (negative feedback). Example: **temperature regulation**. Thermoreceptors in the skin and in the hypothalamus detect a change in temperature and send nerve impulses to the hypothalamus (the control centre), which analyses them and sends instructions to effectors.

- If too hot: effectors cool the body, e.g. **vasodilation** of skin blood vessels increases blood flow to the surface so heat is lost (and sweating).
- If too cold: **vasoconstriction** reduces blood flow to the surface, hair-erector muscles raise the hairs to trap insulating air, and skeletal muscles contract rapidly (shivering) to generate heat.

questions.question: Construct a flow chart in the space provided, outlining the steps involved in whole organism cloning.
questions.answer:
Flow chart:
1. (a) A **somatic cell** from organism 1 (the donor) is extracted and grown in the laboratory; (b) an **egg cell** from organism 2 is extracted.
2. The **nucleus is removed** from the egg cell with a micropipette (enucleated egg).
3. The somatic cell (or its nucleus) is **inserted into the enucleated egg cell**.
4. An **electric shock** is administered to trigger cell division.
5. The **embryo begins to develop**.
6. The embryo is **implanted into a surrogate mother** (organism 3).
7. After pregnancy, an organism **genetically identical to organism 1** is born.

questions.question: Assess the potential of gene therapy in the treatment of a named disease.
questions.answer:
**Cystic fibrosis** sufferers lack a functional gene for a membrane protein that transports chloride (and so water) across membranes, so thick mucus builds up in the lungs. In gene therapy, an **adenovirus vector** carries a normal copy of the gene to the cells lining the lungs, which then make the missing protein and the main symptom is relieved (a pro).

However, the immune system can respond against the vector, effects are temporary because lung cells are replaced, and other vectors have had little success (cons), so this application has so far had limited impact. In the future, as techniques improve, gene therapy has great potential to treat a range of genetic diseases.

questions.question:
Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a group of viruses that infect the skin and mucous membranes of humans. HPV viruses are classified into different serotypes based on the DNA sequences of their viral genomes. Each HPV type is identified by a specific number (e.g. HPV-16, HPV-18).

HPV types can cause changes in the cells of the cervix, leading to the development of precancerous lesions. If these lesions are left untreated, they may progress to invasive cervical cancer.

HPV binds to the surface of epithelial cells and gains entry via endocytosis. Once inside the cell it introduces its viral DNA into the cell's nucleus. It uses the host cell's machinery to produce a viral E6 protein.

With reference to protein synthesis, explain how infection of high-risk HPV strains can lead to cervical cancer.
questions.answer:
High-risk strains (HPV-16 and HPV-18) integrate their DNA into the host cell's genome, so the viral E6 gene is expressed.

*Transcription:* the host's RNA polymerase makes E6 mRNA by adding complementary RNA nucleotides (A, U, C, G) to the growing RNA strand.

*Translation:* the mRNA moves to a ribosome, where tRNAs bring amino acids according to the mRNA codons. Peptide bonds join the amino acids until a stop codon is reached, and the polypeptide folds into the functional E6 oncoprotein.

E6 targets the **p53 tumour suppressor protein** and causes its degradation. p53 normally regulates the cell cycle (halting it at checkpoints to allow repair), triggers **apoptosis** if damage is too severe, and promotes **DNA repair**. Without p53, cells with damaged DNA keep dividing, mutations accumulate, and uncontrolled cell proliferation leads to cervical cancer.

questions.question:
The graph shows the ten-year cumulative incidence rate of cervical precancer by different HPV serotypes. Patients were tested for HPV at the beginning of the 10-year period.

Analyse the trends shown in the data.
questions.answer:
HPV-16 and HPV-18 carry a much higher risk of cervical precancer than other HPV types, and a far higher risk than HPV-negative women.

HPV-16 showed the largest early rise, from 0 to about 11% in the first 15 months, and continued to rise to about 20% by about 87 months. HPV-18 rose from about 0 to 10% between 15 and 39 months, stayed constant until about 75 months and then rose to 15%. Other HPV types stayed low (about 1-2% from about 27 months), and HPV-negative women stayed at about 0% throughout.

Implication: testing for HPV-16 and HPV-18 identifies the women at the highest risk, who need the closest monitoring.

questions.question:
Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a group of viruses that infect the skin and mucous membranes of humans. HPV viruses are classified into different serotypes based on the DNA sequences of their viral genomes. Each HPV type is identified by a specific number (e.g. HPV-16, HPV-18).

HPV types can cause changes in the cells of the cervix, leading to the development of precancerous lesions. If these lesions are left untreated, they may progress to invasive cervical cancer.

HPV binds to the surface of epithelial cells and gains entry via endocytosis. Once inside the cell it introduces its viral DNA into the cell's nucleus. It uses the host cell's machinery to produce a viral E6 protein.

A vaccine has been developed to protect against infection with HPV. Describe how giving this vaccine leads to the production of antibodies against HPV.
questions.answer: The vaccine contains HPV **antigens**. Antigen-presenting cells (e.g. macrophages) take up the antigen and display it on their **MHC** markers. A specific **helper T cell** detects the antigen and stimulates a specific **B cell** that recognises the same antigen. The B cell divides to form clones and differentiates into **plasma cells**, which produce antibodies against HPV, and **memory cells**.

questions.question:
The graph shows the cumulative incidence of invasive cervical cancer according to HPV vaccination status.

Account for the differences in incidence of cervical cancer among the 3 cohorts.
questions.answer:
Incidence is about zero before age 21 because HPV is sexually transmitted and few young women have been exposed for long.

The **unvaccinated** cohort has the highest incidence: with no immunity, HPV can infect cells and trigger uncontrolled proliferation. Those **vaccinated at 17-30** have lower incidence than the unvaccinated but much higher than those vaccinated earlier, because some had already been exposed to HPV before vaccination, and the vaccine does not prevent progression of existing infections as effectively. Those **vaccinated before 17** have the lowest incidence, because the vaccine is most effective when given before exposure to HPV, so immunity (memory cells) is in place before infection.

questions.answer: Denature (heat to separate strands, II), anneal primers at a lower temperature (I), extend with DNA polymerase (IV), then repeat for many cycles to amplify (III).
options: I, II, III, IV
I, II, IV, III
II, I, IV, III
II, I, III, IV

questions.question:

questions.question:
Some organisms reproduce sexually, others asexually.

Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of asexual reproduction.
questions.answer: **Advantage:** there is no need to find or attract a mate (so it is fast and energy-efficient, and a population can build up rapidly). **Disadvantage:** offspring are genetically identical, so there is little genetic diversity in the population, and the whole population is vulnerable to a single disease or environmental change.

questions.question: Compare the structure and location of DNA in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
questions.answer: In eukaryotes the DNA is in **linear chromosomes** (wound around histones) inside a membrane-bound **nucleus**. In prokaryotes the DNA is a **circular** chromosome located in a region of the cell called the **nucleoid** (no nucleus). Prokaryotes may also have extrachromosomal DNA in plasmids, whereas eukaryotes have mtDNA in mitochondria (and cpDNA in chloroplasts).

questions.question: Construct a table to compare and contrast the features of meiosis and mitosis.
questions.answer:
| Feature | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | growth, repair, asexual reproduction | production of gametes |
| Where | body (somatic) cells | gonads (germline cells) |
| Number of divisions | one | two |
| Number of daughter cells | two | four |
| Ploidy of daughter cells | diploid ($2n$) | haploid ($n$) |
| Genetic make-up of daughter cells | identical to the parent cell | genetically different (crossing over, independent assortment) |
| Crossing over | does not occur | occurs in prophase I |

questions.question:
Describe the role of the following in gene cloning:

Ligase, plasmid, restriction enzyme, vector
questions.answer:
- **Restriction enzyme:** cuts the DNA at a specific recognition sequence, to cut out the target gene and to open the plasmid, leaving complementary sticky ends.
- **Plasmid:** a small circular piece of bacterial DNA into which the target gene is inserted; it replicates in the host so the gene is copied.
- **Ligase:** joins the target gene to the plasmid by bonding the sugar-phosphate backbones (sealing the gaps) to form recombinant DNA.
- **Vector:** carries the recombinant DNA (gene) into the host cell (e.g. a plasmid or virus), where it is replicated and expressed.

questions.question:

questions.answer: A **waxy cuticle** on the leaves creates a barrier that traps or blocks pathogens, so they cannot enter the plant. (Also: thick bark is a barrier to pathogens; formation of galls limits the spread of pathogens.)

questions.question:
White clover (*Trifolium repens*) reproduces asexually from a runner that grows along the soil surface. The connected new plants are called ramets. The white clover plant in the diagram is producing ramets in the direction left to right. The fully grown ramets are numbered 1 to 7, from the youngest ramet to the oldest ramet.

Scientists hypothesised that when white clover ramets are damaged by caterpillars of *Spodoptera exigua*, the damaged ramets stimulate other ramets to defend themselves against attack by the caterpillars. The experiment used two genetically identical runners, A and B. In Stage 1, ramets 6 and 7 of Runner A were enclosed in a cage for four days; ramets 6 and 7 of Runner B were each caged with a caterpillar that was left on for four days (30% of leaf surfaces were eaten). In Stage 2, ramets 1 and 5 were cut off each runner and placed in a Petri dish, a caterpillar was released between the two ramets and allowed to feed freely, and after two days the leaf surface area eaten on each ramet was measured.

What is the role of Runner A?
questions.answer: Runner A is the **control**: it is treated the same way but without caterpillar damage, so the effect of the independent variable (earlier damage by caterpillars) can be compared.

After the experiments, the contents of the leaves were analysed. Significantly higher quantities of phenolic acid were found in the young ramets from Runner B. questions.question: Assess the effect of cell replication processes on the genetic code and the continuity of a species.
questions.answer:
**Maintaining the genetic code:** before mitosis and meiosis, DNA is replicated semi-conservatively using complementary base pairing, so each daughter cell receives an exact copy of the genetic code. Mitosis produces genetically identical cells, which maintains the code for growth and repair, and for asexual reproduction.

**Variation:** meiosis produces gametes with half the chromosomes. Crossing over (swapping segments between homologous chromosomes in prophase I) and independent assortment of chromosomes produce new combinations of alleles, and random fertilisation adds more variation. Occasional errors in replication (mutations) add new alleles.

**Assessment for continuity:** accurate copying preserves successful genetic information from one generation to the next, while meiosis gives the genetic variation on which natural selection acts, so some individuals survive environmental change and reproduce. Together they ensure the continuity of the species, although asexual reproduction by mitosis alone leaves a population vulnerable because it lacks variation.

questions.question:
The graphs show different information about the effectiveness of antibiotics as a treatment strategy for infectious disease (deaths from infectious disease 1930-2000, and the increase in antibiotic resistance 1999-2008).

Using the information provided in the graphs and your knowledge, discuss the effectiveness of antibiotics as a treatment strategy for infectious diseases.
questions.answer:
Antibiotics kill bacteria (or stop them reproducing), so they treat bacterial infections. The first graph shows deaths from infectious disease fell from about 200 per 100 000 people in 1930 to about 25 by about 1955, after penicillin was first used in 1942, so antibiotics were very effective (although hygiene and vaccination also contributed). The rate has stayed at about 25-50 since then, with a slight rise in the 1980s-90s.

The second graph shows the percentage of bacteria resistant to antibiotics rising between 1999 and 2008 (e.g. ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin from about 4% to a peak of about 22% in 2006, other antibiotics from about 1-3% to about 5-8%). Overuse leads to natural selection of resistant bacteria, so antibiotics are becoming less effective. Overall, antibiotics have been highly effective, but resistance threatens their future effectiveness, and they do not work on viruses.

questions.question:

Explain why the trait is not sex-linked.
questions.answer:
- **Not Y-linked:** females (individuals 3 and 11) have the trait, but they do not have a Y chromosome.
- **Not X-linked dominant:** an affected male passes his X chromosome (with the dominant allele) to all his daughters, so all daughters would be affected. Individual 4 has the trait but his daughter, individual 9, does not.
- (X-linked recessive is excluded because the allele is dominant.)

So the trait must be autosomal dominant.

The pedigree for a particular trait is shown. The allele for the trait is dominant.

Identify the genotype of Individual 1. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.answer: **Aa** (heterozygous). He has the trait, so he has at least one dominant allele $A$. His children 5 and 6 do not have the trait ($aa$), and each must have received an $a$ allele from him (as their mother, individual 2, is $aa$).

If Individuals 7 and 8 were to have another child, what is the likelihood of the child possessing the trait? Use a Punnett square to illustrate your answer.
questions.answer:
Individual 7 has the trait; his mother (5) is $aa$, so he is **Aa**. Individual 8 does not have the trait: **aa**.

| | $a$ | $a$ |
|---|---|---|
| $A$ | $Aa$ | $Aa$ |
| $a$ | $aa$ | $aa$ |

Probability of a child with the trait = $\frac{2}{4} = \mathbf{50\%}$.

questions.question: Scientists have used biotechnology to create herbicide resistant strains of canola. Explain one advantage of using biotechnology in place of artificial pollination, and explain the potential impact of biotechnology in farming on genetic diversity.
questions.answer:
**Advantage:** biotechnology can introduce a specific desired gene (e.g. herbicide resistance) directly into the crop in one generation, whereas artificial pollination relies on cross-breeding and takes many generations of selection (and unwanted traits are transferred along with the desired one). It is therefore faster and more precise, and can transfer genes between species.

**Impact on genetic diversity:** if farmers grow only a few genetically modified (identical) strains, genetic diversity in crops decreases, and traditional varieties could be lost, so the crop is more vulnerable to a new disease or pest or to environmental change. Transgenes can also spread to wild relatives, and herbicide-resistant weeds could develop.

questions.question:
A student investigated the effectiveness of hand washing. They recruited thirty students who then deliberately contaminated their hands with hard surfaces such as hand rails, desks and door knobs in the classrooms. The students were then randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) no hand washing, (2) hand washing with tap water or (3) hand washing with soap and tap water. Instructions were given as to how to wash their hands and for what length of time. Swabs were then taken from the volunteers' hands and transferred to agar plates. The plates were incubated at 30 °C for 48 hours. The percentage coverage of two types of bacteria that are found in the intestines of animals was calculated and recorded in the table.

| Hand washing technique | Percent of sample with *Enterococcus* spp. bacteria (%) | Percent of sample with *Enterobacter amnigenus* bacteria (%) |
|---|---|---|
| No hand washing | 30 | 12 |
| Water | 15 | 3 |
| Water and soap | 5 | 3 |

Draw an appropriate graph of the results.
questions.answer: A **column graph** with handwashing technique on the x-axis, percentage of sample with bacteria (%) on the y-axis (scale 0-35), two different shaded columns for each technique (*Enterococcus* and *Enterobacter*), plotted correctly and with a key.

questions.question:
A student investigated the effectiveness of hand washing. They recruited thirty students who then deliberately contaminated their hands with hard surfaces such as hand rails, desks and door knobs in the classrooms. The students were then randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) no hand washing, (2) hand washing with tap water or (3) hand washing with soap and tap water. Instructions were given as to how to wash their hands and for what length of time. Swabs were then taken from the volunteers' hands and transferred to agar plates. The plates were incubated at 30 °C for 48 hours. The percentage coverage of two types of bacteria that are found in the intestines of animals was calculated and recorded in the table.

| Hand washing technique | Percent of sample with *Enterococcus* spp. bacteria (%) | Percent of sample with *Enterobacter amnigenus* bacteria (%) |
|---|---|---|
| No hand washing | 30 | 12 |
| Water | 15 | 3 |
| Water and soap | 5 | 3 |

Explain the results in the graph.
questions.answer:
Washing reduced bacterial growth for both bacteria, and **soap and water was the most effective**. *Enterococcus* fell from 30% (no washing) to 15% with water and 5% with soap and water (an 83% reduction). Soap lowers the surface tension and breaks down the oily film/membranes, lifting bacteria off the skin so they are rinsed away.

For *Enterobacter amnigenus* the reduction was from 12% to 3% with water alone, and there was no further reduction with soap (3%), so water alone was as effective as soap for this bacterium, which suggests that rinsing is the key step for it (it is more easily removed).

questions.question:
Protein synthesis includes the processes of transcription and translation.

Describe the steps in transcription.
questions.answer: Transcription occurs in the nucleus. The enzyme **helicase** unwinds and unzips a section of the DNA (a gene), and one strand acts as the template. **RNA polymerase** moves along the template strand and joins free RNA nucleotides by complementary base pairing (A-U, T-A, C-G, G-C) to form a strand of **mRNA**. The mRNA detaches and leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore, and the DNA re-forms its double helix.

questions.question:
Protein synthesis includes the processes of transcription and translation.

Assess the significance of a mutation in a non-coding section of DNA.
questions.answer: Non-coding DNA does not code for amino acids, so a mutation there usually has **no effect on the protein or the phenotype**, so it is often neutral and not significant. However, some non-coding sequences have functions (e.g. promoters, regulatory sequences, introns containing splice sites), so a mutation in them can change gene expression or how the mRNA is spliced and so affect the phenotype. Mutations in non-coding DNA are also useful as markers for tracing ancestry, and can accumulate over generations. Overall, most such mutations have little effect, but some can be significant.

questions.question:
The diagram represents a part of protein synthesis (a ribosome on an mRNA strand, with tRNAs bringing amino acids to form a polypeptide; the structures X and Y are labelled).

Identify the structures labelled X and Y in the diagram, and the location in which the process takes place.
questions.answer: **X:** tRNA (transfer RNA). **Y:** ribosome. **Location:** the cytoplasm (translation).

questions.question:
The diagram represents a part of protein synthesis (a ribosome on an mRNA strand, with tRNAs bringing amino acids to form a polypeptide; the structures X and Y are labelled).

Describe the purpose of mRNA in this process.
questions.answer: mRNA carries the genetic code (a copy of the gene) from the DNA in the nucleus to the ribosome in the cytoplasm. The sequence of its codons determines the order of the amino acids brought by tRNA, and so the sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide.

questions.question:
Zika fever is a rapidly emerging viral disease. It is most commonly transferred from one person to another through the bite of an infected *Aedes* mosquito but can also be transferred from an infected pregnant woman to her foetus, through sexual activity and blood transfusions.

Zika fever in people was first discovered in Uganda in 1947. It was thought that a bite from a mosquito had transferred the virus from monkeys to humans. Since then, it has spread slowly across the globe, with outbreaks most recently in the Americas in 2015 and 2016.

The symptoms of Zika fever are usually mild, ranging from rash, headache, joint and muscle pain to fever. Approximately 80% of infected humans do not show symptoms. Infection of pregnant women, however, can cause severe defects in their babies.

When scientists attempt to identify a particular disease, they can look for specific antibodies in infected humans. Scientists trying to identify Zika infections found that testing for the antibodies produced against the Zika virus often gave them incorrect results. This was because the antibody tests that had been developed could not always identify the difference between the antibodies produced against the Zika virus and the antibodies produced against other viruses.

The graph shows the number of Zika virus cases across the regions of Brazil during 2016.

Describe the trend shown in the graph.
questions.answer: The graph shows the number of Zika cases in each of five Brazilian regions in 2016. Cases rose rapidly to a peak at about week 8-10 (more than 8000 cases in the Northeast region, the highest, with the Southeast and North lower) and then fell significantly after about week 20, to very low numbers by about week 30 onwards.
